docs.title: Crossroads Council
docs.text:
The Crossroads Council is the civic government of Trystn.

Its responsibilities reflect the town’s purpose as a road and caravan hub.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
The Council oversees:

  • Road maintenance
  • Toll schedules
  • Caravan yards
  • Market rules
  • Bridge and culvert repair
  • Escort licensing
  • Traffic during major trade periods
  • Disputes between traveling merchants

Elian Thorne serves as Roadwarden and presides from Tollhouse Commons.

docs.title: Political Character
docs.text:
The Council tends to judge policy by whether people and goods can still move.

It is less interested in ceremony than in keeping one delayed caravan from blocking every road behind it.

docs.title: Kylor Moot
docs.text:
The Kylor Moot is the practical civic government of Kylor.

Logging families, fishers, boat owners, timber factors, and experienced craftspeople dominate its decisions.

Derran Pike serves as Harbor Reeve.

docs.title: Business
docs.text:
The Moot handles:

  • Timber cutting rights
  • Harbor rules
  • Fishing disputes
  • Fire precautions
  • Coastal watch obligations
  • Logging-road maintenance
  • Contracts affecting communal forest access

Formal meetings are held when necessary.

Much of Kylor’s real negotiation happens around Saltwood Market, where everyone affected by a decision eventually has to do business.

docs.title: Mooring Council
docs.text:
The Mooring Council is the chartered civic government of Port Quartz.

It regulates ferries, salvage, warehouses, tariffs, guide licenses, emergency stores, and ordinary civic justice.

Hesta Vane serves as First Mooring and presides from Hall of Moorings.

The council recognizes the Crown but strongly resists attempts by the Aegis Legion to convert emergency military authority into permanent control of the town.

docs.title: Seats and Influence
docs.text:
The Council’s traditional offices divide responsibility among the people who keep the river town functioning: ferry operations, river works, merchant factors, civic wards, and the First Mooring.

Wealth matters in Port Quartz, but so does the ability to keep ferries moving during bad water. A rich merchant who cannot solve a practical river problem may carry less influence than an experienced crew leader.

Hesta Vane chairs the Council without treating it as a personal court.

docs.title: Stone Council
docs.text:
The Stone Council governs Lilya and represents the town’s mine crews, smelters, haulers, craftsmen, and established households.

Maela Torr serves as Stone Reeve and chairs meetings at Stonewake Hall.

The council cooperates with the Aegis Legion on defense but treats local mine law as a civic right rather than a privilege granted by the Crown.

docs.title: Authority
docs.text:
The Council sets mine closures, approves major hauling contracts, maintains emergency food and timber reserves, and settles disputes that cross several mining crews.

Its rulings matter because a careless decision underground can endanger an entire district rather than one household.

Maela Torr chairs meetings but is expected to persuade the other interests rather than simply command them.

docs.title: The Crown of Saros
docs.text:
The Crown of Saros is the legal monarchy centered on Queen Amara and Pyrris.

It is less a single office than the combined authority of the Queen, The Queen’s Council, Crown magistrates, royal charters, and institutions such as The Aegis Legion.

docs.title: Authority
docs.text:
The Crown claims authority over:

  • Realm-wide law
  • Coinage
  • Major treaties
  • High justice
  • Military defense
  • Royal charters
  • Certain taxes and tariffs

Local settlements still govern much of their own daily life.

A town charter can therefore matter almost as much as a distant decree.

docs.title: Present Crisis
docs.text:
The disappearance of Queen Amara has exposed how much legitimacy rested personally upon her.

The Council continues governing.

The Legion continues enforcing Crown law.

Local leaders increasingly ask who, exactly, has the right to expand those powers while the Queen is absent.

docs.title: The House Table
docs.text:
The House Table is the governing council of independent Rore.

The council is dominated by great gaming houses, lenders, brokers, ward representatives, and commercial interests that agree on one principle above all others: Rore should not be governed by the Crown.

Cassia Rook currently serves as First Dealer.

The House Table meets at The Dealhouse and funds common ward guards while allowing individual houses to maintain private security.

docs.title: How Decisions Are Made
docs.text:
The House Table prefers bargains to decrees.

Major gaming houses, lenders, ward interests, and commercial brokers trade support until enough of the city benefits from the same decision to make enforcement practical.

Cassia Rook presides as First Dealer, but a First Dealer who repeatedly damages business can lose support quickly.

The system is messy, wealthy, and deliberately unlike Crown government.

docs.title: Khaz’um
docs.text: The First Dwarves. Their united culture faded during The Wandering, and no confirmed Khaz’um settlement survives.

docs.title: Thar’um
docs.text: The Mountain Keepers and Gem-Seekers. Thar’um delvers maintain deep roads, work Fey-stone, and are the dwarves most frequently encountered by other Sarosiansâ€”when they wish to be encountered.

docs.title: Khaz’armok
docs.text: The Sand Dwarves and Dune-Breakers. Their houses vanished into The Glimmering Expanse during The Scattering after The Great Betrayal; hidden settlements there remain a persistent rumor.

docs.title: Khaz'armok
docs.text: The Khaz’armok are the legendary Sand Dwarves and Dune-Breakers, a clan whose history became inseparable from The Glimmering Expanse. The name now includes stone-shaping houses once recorded separately as the Khaz’dar.

docs.title: The Split
docs.text:
The Great Betrayal began as a dispute among allied Khaz’armok houses over the finest gem their traditions had inherited from the older Khaz’um. Later outsiders treated two sides of the civil war as separate clans and called one of them Khaz’dar.

The feud shattered the old holds. During The Scattering, survivors moved into or through the Glimmering Expanse in search of safety and territory beyond their rivals.

docs.title: Craft
docs.text: Khaz’armok tradition is associated with shaping earth and stone, excavating monumental chambers, building underground roads, and raising fortifications that look grown from the rock itself.

docs.title: Lost Routes
docs.text:
For a time, other Sarosians believed Khaz’armok guides knew how to cross sections of the Expanse that were otherwise nearly impassable.

Trade and communication eventually stopped.

docs.title: Modern Belief
docs.text:
Most people consider the clan lost.

Stories still claim that hidden Khaz’armok settlements survive among glass formations, buried fortresses, or deep desert delves.

No modern expedition has produced proof accepted by the wider realm.

docs.title: Khaz'um
docs.text:
The Khaz’um are remembered as the earliest dwarves of Saros.

Little direct history survives.

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text:
Dwarven tradition credits the Khaz’um with beginning The Wandering, the great period of exploration during which dwarven communities spread across the mountains and discovered powerful Fey-Lines.

Broken chronicles also credit their deepest expeditions with discoveries later inherited, hidden, or fought over by the emerging clans. References to a Deep Jewel survive, but their meaning is disputed.

As those communities became more isolated and specialized, new Dwarven Clans developed.

The original Khaz’um identity gradually disappeared.

No modern settlement openly claims to be a surviving pure Khaz’um community, though nearly every major clan traces some part of its ancestry back to them.

Their disappearance is considered cultural rather than a single recorded extinction.

docs.title: Thar'um
docs.text:
The Thar’um are the Mountain Keepers and Gem-Seekers, a dwarven clan formed from traditions once recorded separately as the Tha’run and Vak’dar.

They are the dwarves most frequently seen in the settled parts of Saros, although Thar’um communities reveal themselves, open their gates, and trade only when they choose.

docs.title: Specialty
docs.text:
Thar’um craft focuses on:

  • Gem cutting
  • Magical stone
  • Surveying fey-line convergences
  • Deep mining
  • Fey-stone
  • Structural reinforcement
  • Underground roads, ventilation, and water control
  • Defensive gates and deliberate sealing

Dwarven tradition credits their forebears with developing many of the practices that later became known simply as delving. Their engineers are equally respected for knowing when a dangerous depth must be sealed.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Thar’um traders, engineers, and envoys are encountered throughout Saros, but outsiders rarely see the clan’s deeper holdings. Stories about Thar’um works often end with a sealed door and no explanation.

Old Thar’um markings are especially prized because they can identify magical deposits, stable underground routes, or places that should never be opened again.

docs.title: Bank of Saros
docs.text:
The Bank of Saros is not a separate chain of buildings. It is the banking network operated through every chartered Gambler’s Guild hall.

A depositor can place coin or valuables with one hall, receive a verified account mark or draft, and arrange a withdrawal through another. The Guild profits from fees, exchange rates, loans, storage, and the fact that merchants would rather trust its ledgers than carry a fortune through dangerous country.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Guild halls commonly provide:

  • Coin deposits and withdrawals
  • Secured storage for compact valuables
  • Currency exchange and appraisal
  • Verified drafts honored at another Guild hall
  • Escrow for wagers and contracts
  • Loans backed by property, cargo, or reputation

The Guild does not promise equal service to everyone. Large withdrawals may require notice, identity may be verified by private methods, and a disputed account can be frozen until Guild arbiters decide who is lying.

Every Bank of Saros is also a gambling hall. The Guild insists this concentrates security, trustworthy counting staff, and liquid coin in one place. Critics observe that it also places lenders beside people making poor decisions.

docs.title: Gambler's Guild
docs.text:
The Gambler’s Guild regulates and profits from organized gaming across much of civilized Saros.

Its influence is strongest in Rore. The Guild charters exactly one official gambling hall in any city or town it serves. House games, tavern games, and street wagers may exist, but they are unsanctioned and receive no Guild protection.

Every chartered gambling hall also serves as a Bank of Saros, allowing depositors to move wealth between distant settlements without carrying all of it on the road.

docs.title: What the Guild Does
docs.text:
The Guild is concerned with:

  • Recognized gaming rules
  • House licensing
  • Tournament organization
  • Large wager verification
  • Debt records
  • Professional dealers
  • Arbitration over disputed games
  • Protection against obvious cheating
  • Deposits, secured storage, currency exchange, and verified inter-hall drafts

The Guild’s involvement does not make gambling safe or fair in every establishment. It means there is someone powerful enough to care when cheating damages the reputation of profitable gaming.

docs.title: Appearance and Habits
docs.text:
Guild professionals tend toward richer, cleaner, and more elaborate dress than ordinary merchants. Tailored coats, immaculate cuffs, fine waistcoats, polished jewelry, house tokens, cards, dice, and discreet banking seals all serve as signs that games and money are being handled under recognized authority.

The effect is controlled rather than gaudy. A successful dealer or banker wants every visible detail to suggest confidence, cleanliness, memory, and command of the room.

docs.title: Rore
docs.text:
In Rore, the Guild is one of several institutions capable of influencing The House Table.

It is wealthy, politically connected, and useful enough that even people who dislike gambling generally prefer it to a city full of entirely unregulated games.

docs.title: Merchant's Guild
docs.text:
The Merchant’s Guild is one of the broadest commercial organizations in Saros.

It does not control all trade, but membership provides recognition, arbitration, contacts, and a shared set of expectations that make long-distance business less dangerous.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
The Guild commonly deals with:

  • Trade standards
  • Weights and measures
  • Contract witnessing
  • Merchant arbitration
  • Caravan partnerships
  • Credit references
  • Warehousing connections
  • Information about dangerous routes

Its influence is strongest in commercial centers such as Goslow, Port Quartz, Trystn, and Soryn’s Crossing.

docs.title: Appearance and Habits
docs.text:
Guild members generally aim to look prosperous, trustworthy, and professionally ornate. Clean layered clothing, quality fabric, well-kept boots, practical traveling coats, stamped seals, ledgers, keys, measuring tools, and restrained jewelry communicate that a merchant can protect both goods and reputation.

The exact display varies by trade. A caravan factor dresses for weather and roads; a hall broker may favor richer fabric and careful ornament. Obvious wealth is useful, but appearing careless with it is not.

docs.title: Politics
docs.text:
The Guild usually prefers stable government because stable roads make money.

That does not mean it blindly supports the Crown.

When tariffs, military seizures, or local corruption threaten commerce, powerful Guild members can resist through delayed shipments, legal challenges, private guards, and coordinated refusal to extend credit.

docs.title: Bloodmarked
docs.text:
The Bloodmarked are one of the most feared pirate factions operating around southern Saros.

They are strongly associated with the waters near Karastos and with attacks that draw the attention of Grymswatch and the Aegis Legion fleet.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Bloodmarked crews are known for aggressive boarding actions and for marking themselves or their ships in ways intended to make identification frightening rather than difficult.

Merchants often use the name broadly for violent raiders even when responsibility has not been proven.

docs.title: Organization
docs.text:
The Bloodmarked are not a single perfectly disciplined navy.

Individual captains possess substantial independence, bound together by shared reputation, alliances, and access to pirate markets.

That flexibility makes them difficult for Admiral Thainan and other Legion commanders to eliminate through a single decisive campaign.

docs.title: Garrisons
docs.text:
Major known Aegis Legion garrisons include:

  • Stonepeak in Pyrris — commanded by General Ironclad
  • Duskpoint outside Goslow — commanded by Vostin The Mighty
  • Mira’s Wall in Grymswatch — naval stronghold of Admiral Thainan
  • The Port Quartz garrison — commanded by Captain Serin Holt

Smaller posts, road stations, signal towers, and temporary patrol camps exist throughout the settled regions of Saros.

The Legion’s legal authority differs according to local charter. A garrison may be militarily dominant without serving as the town’s civil government.

docs.title: The Aegis Legion
docs.text:
The Aegis Legion is the principal military institution of the Crown and the most visible symbol of royal authority outside Pyrris.

Its motto is:

Honor, Heart, Homeland

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Legion is responsible for:

  • Defense of the realm
  • Garrisons in major settlements
  • Patrols along important roads
  • Coastal and naval security
  • Response to monsters or organized raiders
  • Enforcement of serious Crown law
  • Support during disasters and sieges

In many remote places, the arrival of a Legion patrol is the only regular contact people have with the central government.

docs.title: Appearance and Equipment
docs.text:
The Legion presents itself as practical, disciplined, and professional. Armor, clothing, weapons, and insignia are maintained for hard use rather than ceremonial spectacle, although officers and formal guards may wear more polished equipment.

Griffin Riders use lighter functional riding armor, secure harness points, weather protection, and gear designed not to interfere with wings or saddle movement. A griffin and rider are lifelong partners, not interchangeable cavalry equipment issued from a stable.

docs.title: Command
docs.text:
General Ironclad is the supreme military commander.

Important regional officers include:

  • Vostin The Mighty at Duskpoint near Goslow
  • Admiral Thainan at Grymswatch
  • Captain Serin Holt at Port Quartz

The Legion’s authority varies by local charter. A garrison may be powerful without technically being the civil government.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Supporters view the Legion as the reason roads remain open and towns survive attacks from the wilderness.

Critics see an armed institution increasingly willing to decide what the law means for itself.

Both views have become stronger since Queen Amara disappeared.

Without the Queen’s personal authority, Legion commanders are receiving more responsibility while civic leaders, guilds, and The Black Circle question how temporary those powers really are.

docs.title: Garrisons
docs.text:
The largest concentration of Legion forces is associated with Grymswatch and the military establishment at Mira’s Wall.

Smaller garrisons and posts protect major roads, ports, and politically important settlements throughout the realm.

docs.title: The Black Circle
docs.text:
The Black Circle is a loose and deliberately decentralized network built around the belief that no ruler, army, guild, or council possesses an inherent right to own another person’s freedom.

It is not an arm of the Crown, has never worked for The Queen’s Council, and does not recognize the Aegis Legion as a moral authority merely because it carries royal law.

docs.title: Organization
docs.text:
There is no single head of the Black Circle.

The organization consists of:

  • Small chapterhouses
  • Roaming bands
  • Trusted individual contacts
  • Hidden refuges
  • Local cells that may know little about one another

Members can disagree sharply about methods while sharing the same broad suspicion of concentrated authority.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Most members do not wear a uniform.

A traditional sign of membership is a magical black-circle tattoo hidden near the inner crook of the arm. It is invisible under ordinary inspection.

When two members greet by grasping one another’s arms near the elbow, each places a thumb over the other’s hidden mark. Both circles appear beneath their thumbs for the duration of the grip and fade when they release. A painted or ordinary tattoo does not answer the greeting, making the sign difficult to counterfeit.

Because the Circle often operates quietly, ordinary people may know it exists without knowing who belongs to it.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Most members dress like ordinary travelers, laborers, sailors, hunters, merchants, or pilgrims and deliberately blend into local crowds.

The Circle’s best-known visual tradition is a black, weathered, ranger-like cloak. Such cloaks are not an everyday uniform. Roaming bands wear them together mainly when they intend to declare solidarity, escort vulnerable people openly, or make a deliberate show of force.

Even then, practical layers, repaired leather, road gear, and travel stains matter more than menace. The Black Circle sees itself as a defender of free people, not as a brotherhood of threatening assassins.

docs.title: Relationship with the Crown
docs.text:
The Crown and Legion frequently describe Circle members as traitors, seditionists, criminals, or terrorists.

That description is politically useful but incomplete.

Black Circle members have:

  • Protected travelers
  • Defended villages beyond dependable Legion reach
  • Helped people escape abusive authorities
  • Attacked Crown operations they believed violated basic freedoms
  • Smuggled wanted people through checkpoints
  • Fought monsters, pirates, and other threats when no official force was present

The Circle is therefore loved, hated, feared, or quietly tolerated depending on who is telling the story.

docs.title: Queen Amara
docs.text:
The Circle has historically shown more respect toward Queen Amara personally than toward the monarchy as an institution.

Many members believe Amara’s restraint and willingness to forgive prevented the Crown from becoming far worse than it already could have been.

Her disappearance has increased suspicion that the balance between Crown authority and individual freedom is failing.

docs.title: The Legion
docs.text:
Conflict with Aegis Legion is common.

The Circle sees the Legion’s growing emergency powers as proof that military authority always expands when given the chance.

Legion officers see the Circle’s secrecy and willingness to obstruct lawful orders as an invitation to chaos.

Both sides can point to real examples supporting their view.

docs.title: Clarissa
docs.text:
Clarissa is a young human mage and known member of The Black Circle.

She favors dark traveling robes, keeps her blond hair practical, and has an unassuming smile that has repeatedly failed to convince Legion officers she is harmless.

docs.title: Skaggerty
docs.text:
Clarissa was formally banished from Skaggerty after her connection to the Black Circle became impossible for local authorities to ignore.

She still knows people there and is likely to hear village news even when she cannot enter openly.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
The Aegis Legion considers Clarissa troublesome because she is willing to interfere when she believes an order violates basic freedoms.

She is not famous for indiscriminate violence.

Her danger comes from mobility, magic, sympathetic contacts, and a complete lack of respect for an order merely because someone in uniform delivered it.

docs.title: The Prism
docs.text:
The Prism is a secretive draconic cult associated with Silas Voss and his lieutenant Malgrim Darkshade.

Most people in Saros know the name only through rumor, warnings, recovered symbols, or stories about groups searching ancient ruins.

Fewer than one thousand true members are believed to exist, and even that is an uncertain upper limit. The cult’s visible servants, hired agents, intermediaries, and sympathizers are not necessarily initiated members.

docs.title: The Multi-Chromatic Egg
docs.text:
The cult is obsessed with a Sarosian legend concerning the egg of a Multi-Chromatic Dragon.

The story claims that the first being seen by a newly hatched dragon of that kind will be granted a wish of extraordinary power.

The Prism believes the legend literally.

Prism prophecy claims that finding the egg will herald Silas’s return, free him from the Veil of Desolation, and allow him to claim the throne of Saros. This is a statement of cult faith, not an established property of the egg or proof that Silas still lives.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Public stories associate Prism agents with:

  • Searching old ruins
  • Studying dragons
  • Stealing magical relics
  • Recruiting dangerous spellcasters
  • Buying information through intermediaries
  • Operating through cult cells that do not always know one another
  • Carrying small faceted crystals or using restrained prismatic signs

Because the cult is secretive, unrelated crimes are sometimes blamed on it simply because nobody has a better explanation.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Members favor restrained occult clothing rather than bright rainbow display: dark layered robes, practical hoods, matte fabrics, geometric embroidery, and faceted jewelry that reveals color mainly when it catches the light.

Witnesses sometimes describe a faint prismatic glint in a member’s skin. Field agents usually hide obvious cult dress and may pass as scholars, travelers, merchants, or hired spellcasters.

docs.title: Silas Voss
docs.text:
Silas Voss is widely described as the cult’s central figure.

His history with Caelum and Queen Amara reaches back to Mystara and the catastrophe that preceded the Arrival.

The cult continues to recognize Silas as its true leader and reveres him with an intensity that often resembles worship. No reliable witness has seen him since Caelum’s End, however, and no one outside the cult can establish whether he survived the fall.

Malgrim Darkshade is the highest-ranking Prism operative publicly known to be active. Whether she receives instructions from Silas, interprets an older command, or governs in his absence is unknown.

docs.title: Malgrim Darkshade
docs.text: Malgrim Darkshade is the most frequently named lieutenant of Silas Voss and is commonly described as second only to him within The Prism. She is the highest-ranking operative whose continued activity is known beyond the cult.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Malgrim is a tall, pale elf who favors black layered clothing, restrained faceted adornment, and a deep hood.

Her white hair, milk-white eyes, and faintly refractive skin make her memorable to the few people who claim to have seen her closely.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Stories describe Malgrim as:

  • Highly intelligent
  • Patient
  • Skilled in forbidden or obscure magic
  • Willing to use other people as tools
  • More interested in knowledge and influence than devotion for its own sake

Even people who believe Silas is the true center of the Prism often describe Malgrim as the person most likely to understand the cult’s complicated magical work.

docs.title: Silas Voss
docs.text:
Malgrim publicly serves Silas Voss, although no reliable account establishes that she has communicated with him since Caelum’s End.

Rumor portrays the relationship as loyalty mixed with ambition.

Whether she truly intends to surpass her master or whether that story is simply how outsiders explain her independence is unknown.

docs.title: Silas Voss
docs.text:
Silas Voss is a human wizard tied to both the destruction that preceded Caelum’s Arrival and the modern cult called The Prism. His current fate is unknown.

He was once a student of Caelum and Amara.

docs.title: Mystara
docs.text:
By the time Caelum and Amara understood the scale of Silas’s ambitions, he had already begun dangerous work involving the outer planes and immortality.

Later Sarosian accounts blame those experiments for helping create the catastrophe from which Caelum’s people fled.

docs.title: Immortality
docs.text:
Silas is believed to have achieved a form of immortality at a terrible cost.

The condition is often called the Veil of Desolation.

Stories say it severed him from ordinary joy, affection, and other positive feeling while corrupting the magic he once used more freely.

Whether every detail of that description is literally true is impossible to verify.

docs.title: The Prism
docs.text:
Silas is associated with the search for a Multi-Chromatic Dragon’s egg.

The cult believes such a dragon can grant a wish to the first being it sees after hatching.

A wish powerful enough to alter an immortal curse would explain Silas’s interest.

docs.title: Caelum’s End
docs.text:
Roughly eight hundred years ago, Caelum and Amara made a final attempt at the northern peak now called Caelum’s End to bring their former pupil back from the brink of evil.

Only Amara witnessed the end. Caelum and Silas both went over the frozen edge into the sea.

Amara returned alone. Neither man has been reliably seen since, and no accepted evidence proves that either survived.

Amara has never given a complete public account of what caused the fall.

Most Sarosians believe master and pupil fought their way to the end of the world and dragged one another over the cliffs. Court histories preserve Amara’s claim that the journey began as a final attempt at redemption.

The Prism nevertheless continues to recognize Silas as its true leader. Its members believe the recovery of the Multi-Chromatic Dragon’s egg will cause his return, remove his curse, and permit him to claim the throne. The prophecy is evidence of Prism belief, not of Silas’s survival.

docs.title: The Queen's Council
docs.text:
The Queen’s Council is the five-member body that manages much of the daily government of Saros from The Radiant Citadel in Pyrris.

Even before Queen Amara disappeared, it was an open secret that the Council handled most of the machinery that actually kept the realm functioning.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
The five seats divide the broad work of government:

  • General Ironclad — military command and defense
  • Archmage Starweaver — arcane affairs
  • Lord Goldhaven — treasury and finance
  • Ambassador Skylark — diplomacy and public relations
  • Spymaster Shadowcloak — intelligence and espionage

Amara traditionally stood above these offices as monarch and final authority.

docs.title: Public Reputation
docs.text:
The Council has never inspired the personal affection that Amara often did.

Supporters argue that five specialists have kept a difficult realm functioning across enormous distances and dangerous country.

Critics argue that the Queen’s kindness allowed unelected officials to accumulate power with very little public scrutiny.

Both sides agree that the Council does a great deal more than simply offer advice.

docs.title: The Queen’s Absence
docs.text:
Since Amara vanished, the Council has continued issuing decrees and directing the government in her name.

Some citizens praise that continuity.

Others believe the Council is:

  • Concealing what happened
  • Using the crisis to enlarge its authority
  • Unable to control the increasingly independent Legion
  • Directly responsible for the Queen’s disappearance

No accusation has been publicly proven.

The longer Amara remains missing, the harder it becomes for the Council to rely on her legitimacy.
