docs.title: A Brief Saros History
docs.text:
Just over fourteen centuries ago, the wizard Caelum made a desperate wish to save the remnants of his people from catastrophe in their former world of Mystara.

Nearly one thousand beings were carried to Saros.

They did not find a thriving human kingdom waiting for them. The old civilizations of Saros had already shattered. Ruins, abandoned roads, sealed delves, haunted battlefields, and isolated surviving communities covered a land that was beautiful, magical, and profoundly dangerous.

The newcomers possessed agricultural methods, military organization, crafts, and habits of settlement that differed greatly from those of the scattered Sarosian peoples they encountered. Over the following centuries, their communities absorbed, allied with, displaced, and intermarried with surviving inhabitants. The settlements familiar to modern travelers grew from that long period of consolidation.

docs.title: The Realm Today
docs.text:
The inhabited portions of Saros are concentrated around fortified towns, ports, farms, mines, and roads. Vast areas between them remain unsafe or poorly understood.

Goslow is the largest city and commercial center of the realm. The capital, Pyrris, is much smaller: a fortified royal settlement built around The Radiant Citadel high above Bishop’s Bay.

The realm is formally ruled by the elven Queen Amara, widow of Caelum. Amara has held the throne for roughly eight hundred years, since Caelum and Silas Voss both went over the frozen edge at Caelum’s End during their last confrontation.

For much of her reign she was regarded as benevolent, unusually forgiving, and personally distant from the everyday machinery of government. The Queen’s Council handled much of that machinery, and it has long been an open secret that the five councillors exercise enormous practical power.

Amara has now been missing for months.

The Council continues governing in her name. The Aegis Legion has taken increasingly broad responsibility for order. Distrust of the Crown is growing, and groups such as The Black Circle are becoming more openly critical of Legion authority.

docs.title: Old Saros
docs.text:
Nearly everything beyond settled roads sits upon older history.

Ancient warp-gates can sometimes be found among the ruins. Some can still be awakened.

The Fey-Lines influence magic, living things, and the hidden places of elves and dwarves.

No one knows with certainty what lies beyond the surrounding seas.

Elven traditions call the world Aiy-Vana, “Beautiful to Behold.”

Dwarven traditions call it Daron, “Deep Knowledge.”

Saros has twin suns, strange moons, old monsters, and more ruins than its present population could ever hope to reclaim.

docs.title: Persistent Rumors
docs.text:
Stories repeated across the realm include:

  • Werewolves appearing beneath red moons
  • Forgotten dwarven delves beneath the mountains
  • Hidden elven domains in ancient forests
  • A Great Sphinx somewhere in The Glimmering Expanse
  • The secretive cult called The Prism
  • A legendary multi-chromatic dragon egg capable of granting a wish to the first being seen by its hatchling

docs.title: Ages of Saros
docs.text: Sarosian historians divide the world’s past into three broad Ages. The boundaries are partly historical and partly cultural; the farther back an Age lies, the less confidently anyone can separate record from legend.

docs.title: 1st Age — The First Breaths
docs.text:
There is no dependable written history from the First Age.

Tradition says dragons ruled before the younger peoples of Saros had established kingdoms of their own. The greatest surviving story tells of a catastrophic war among dragons powerful enough to permanently reshape the continent.

The clearest supposed evidence is central Saros:

  • The Glimmering Expanse, a vast desert of sand and jagged glass
  • The Wyrm Scar, the enormous wound that nearly divides the continent in two

Whether every detail of the dragon war is true is unknowable. The land itself is difficult to explain any other way.

docs.title: 2nd Age — The Great Tribulation
docs.text:
The Second Age begins with the first humanoid civilizations remembered in surviving Sarosian tradition.

Magic was poorly understood by the earliest human tribes. Competition, mistrust, and betrayal eventually produced wars whose scale became legendary.

This Age saw:

  • The rise and destruction of the Storm Knights
  • Wars among early human kingdoms
  • The dead later associated with Blackwater Bog
  • The creation of the enormous burial mounds called The Urmong Barrows
  • Elven discovery and cultivation of the Fey-Lines
  • Elven withdrawal into hidden woodland domains
  • The rise of the Dwarven Clans and their great Delves
  • The Great Betrayal and the later Scattering of the Khaz’armok

By the end of the Age, organized human civilization had largely collapsed. Dwarven kingdoms had sealed or lost many delves. Elven populations had withdrawn from open political life. Survivors remained, but the old network of states and cities was gone.

docs.title: 3rd Age — Caelum’s Arrival
docs.text:
Just over 1,400 years ago, Caelum’s wish brought nearly one thousand refugees from Mystara to Saros.

Their arrival did not create civilization from nothing, but it transformed the scattered world they found.

The newcomers brought different methods of:

  • Agriculture
  • Fortification
  • Warfare
  • Record keeping
  • Shipbuilding
  • Trade
  • Civic administration

They encountered surviving Sarosians living in isolated settlements, hidden communities, and the remnants of older cultures.

docs.title: The Years of Gathering
docs.text:
The first generations established defended settlements, cleared roads, recovered farmland, and made contact with surviving peoples.

The communities that would eventually become places such as Goslow and Port Quartz began to take recognizable form.

docs.title: The Chartering Centuries
docs.text: Settlements expanded into towns. Trade routes stabilized. Guilds and civic charters appeared. The Crown’s influence spread along roads, rivers, and ports rather than across every mile of wilderness.

docs.title: Caelum’s End
docs.text:
Roughly eight centuries ago, Caelum and Amara took their former pupil Silas Voss to the frozen northern peak now called Caelum’s End in one final attempt to turn him away from evil.

Only Amara witnessed what followed. Caelum and Silas both went over the edge into the sea. Neither has been reliably seen since.

Amara returned alone to Pyrris, where she assumed the throne of her husband.

The cause and manner of the fall, and the ultimate fate of both men, remain uncertain because Amara has never given a complete public account.

For a detailed population and settlement chronology of the Third Age, see Sarosian Timeline.

docs.title: The Amaran Reign
docs.text:
Amara’s eight-century reign brought long periods of comparative stability.

The settlements expanded, the Aegis Legion became the principal military institution of the realm, civic charters matured, and trade became routine enough for ordinary people to build lives rather than merely survive.

The realm never fully conquered the wilderness.

Ruins, monsters, broken magical regions, old wars, pirates, and the sheer difficulty of travel kept Saros sparsely settled compared with the amount of land it claims.

docs.title: The Fraying Present
docs.text:
The Third Age has not officially ended.

Amara has been missing for months.

The Queen’s Council governs in her absence. Legion officers possess growing local power. The Black Circle increasingly condemns Crown authority. Old factions are moving again.

Whether later historians will mark this period as the end of the Third Age has yet to be decided.

docs.title: Griffin Riders
docs.text:
True Griffin Riders are bonded companions to their griffins rather than owners of interchangeable cavalry mounts.

The Aegis Legion maintains the most visible organized riders in modern Saros, but the tradition is not exclusive to the Crown. Riders of any faction normally follow the same dangerous path to Vy’Tungavor.

docs.title: Claiming a Griffin
docs.text:
A prospective rider travels into the high peaks and attempts to claim a fresh hatchling. Finding an unhatched egg is exceptionally rare and is not the normal route into the tradition.

An adult griffin is not simply captured, broken, and reassigned. The lasting bond begins while the creature is very young.

docs.title: Pair-Bond
docs.text:
Griffins bond intensely with their handlers and require regular proximity. Once fixed, that loyalty is effectively non-transferable.

Long separation can cause agitation, refusal to feed, aggression, illness, or attempts to escape and find the bonded rider. The rider is affected less uniformly, but experienced riders describe separation as physically and emotionally distressing.

The relationship lasts for life. A rider whose griffin dies is not routinely issued another hatchling, and a griffin whose rider dies rarely accepts a replacement.

docs.title: Growth and Scale
docs.text:
A newly claimed hatchling requires years of care before it can carry a rider.

A standard mature Sarosian riding griffin is larger-bodied than a draft horse and usually spans roughly 18–22 feet from wingtip to wingtip. Exceptional heavy or tandem-capable griffins may reach 22–26 feet.

docs.title: Saddles and Flight
docs.text:
The saddle is positioned around the griffin’s natural center of balance near the shoulder and wing-root region. Exact placement varies with the animal’s build and the intended load.

The rider’s thighs straddle the torso and the legs rest naturally along the flanks without passing through the wings or obstructing their movement. Sarosian practice does not insist that every rider sit rigidly in front of or behind the wings.

docs.title: Feeding and Care
docs.text:
Mature griffins consume tremendous quantities of food. A working roost needs handlers, butchers or fishing contracts, drainage, secure resting space, tack repair, and room for safe takeoff and landing.

This cost naturally limits their number. Griffins excel at scouting, patrol, command travel, and urgent communication, but cannot replace ships or wagons carrying bulk cargo.

Ordinary flight covers roughly 70–100 miles in a day when weather and rest permit. An emergency courier may cover 120–150 miles, but such exertion is not a sustainable daily routine. See Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population for the wider travel model.

docs.title: Sarosian Timeline
docs.text:
The Sarosian Timeline organizes the known history in Ages of Saros and gives the Third Age a working demographic scale. Dates in the modern record are measured After Arrival (AA), beginning when Caelum’s wish carried the Wanderers from Mystara to Saros.

The present is approximately 1,400 AA.

Dates before the Arrival are reconstructed from ruins, oral traditions, elven memory, dwarven records, and later copies. They should be treated as increasingly uncertain the farther back they reach.

docs.title: Population at a Glance
docs.text:
Known Saros holds approximately 300,000 inhabitants. The number is a useful estimate, not a complete census.

Time Approximate Known Population Demographic Character Arrival, 0 AA 8,000–10,000 Nearly 1,000 Wanderers plus scattered surviving Sarosians 200 AA 13,000–17,000 Fortified farms and the first stable charter towns 600 AA 35,000–50,000 A connected realm exists; Caelum’s reign ends 900 AA 80,000–100,000 Amaran institutions and southern trade expand 1,200 AA 190,000–220,000 Long-distance trade and settlement reach their broadest growth Present, about 1,400 AA 280,000–320,000 Working canon: approximately 300,000

These figures describe long trends rather than smooth growth. Saros has repeatedly lost whole communities to famine, sickness, monsters, war, magical contamination, piracy, isolation, and failed roads.

The Council’s latest official count claims only 260,000–275,000 people. It badly undercounts:

  • Hidden elven communities
  • Sealed or private dwarven holds
  • Pirate settlements
  • Nomadic peoples
  • Remote islands and fishing camps
  • Unchartered villages
  • Communities that refuse Crown taxation
  • Travelers and displaced people between settlements

docs.title: People of Modern Saros
docs.text:
The following proportions are useful realm-wide estimates. Individual settlements can differ dramatically.

People Approximate Population Share Humans 255,000 85% Dwarves 12,000 4% Halflings 12,000 4% Elves 6,000 2% Orcs and half-orcs 6,000 2% Other peoples 9,000 3% Total 300,000 100%

These categories reflect census habits more than clean ancestry. Fourteen centuries of movement, alliance, adoption, and intermarriage make many local identities more important than census labels.

docs.title: First Age — The First Breaths
docs.text:
No dependable continuous calendar survives from the First Age.

Later traditions agree on only a broad sequence:

  • Dragons dominated the earliest remembered world.
  • Younger peoples existed but left few records that modern historians can date.
  • Rival dragons fought a war vast enough to alter the land itself.
  • The region now called The Glimmering Expanse became a waste of sand and jagged glass.
  • The Wyrm Scar tore across central Saros.
  • Dragon rule ended, fractured, or withdrew beyond ordinary history.

Modern historians call the era The First Breaths because nearly every people places its earliest origin stories somewhere within it. The name does not imply a single creation story.

docs.title: What Survives
docs.text:
• Dragon bones and structures too large for later builders
  • Glass fields with incompatible magical signatures
  • Fragments of prehumanoid or unidentifiable writing
  • Oral traditions preserved by elves, dwarves, and isolated communities
  • Relics that do not respond consistently to modern magic

No population estimate is credible for this Age.

docs.title: Second Age — The Great Tribulation
docs.text: The Second Age begins with the first humanoid civilizations that can be recognized in surviving Sarosian tradition. It ends with their political collapse before Caelum’s Arrival.

docs.title: Early Second Age
docs.text:
• Human tribes established permanent farming settlements and river communities.
  • Elves discovered, mapped, and cultivated portions of the Fey-Lines.
  • The Khaz’um, remembered as the First Dwarves, explored deep mineral regions.
  • The Wandering produced new dwarven holds and the later clan traditions.
  • Magic spread faster than the customs needed to govern its use.
  • Regional rulers reused First Age sites without understanding all of them.

docs.title: The Rise of Realms
docs.text:
• Human kingdoms built roads, fortifications, burial grounds, and coastal settlements.
  • The Storm Knights became a major military and learned order.
  • Elven domains withdrew behind guarded woodland borders as human wars intensified.
  • Dwarven delves expanded around mineral wealth and fey-line convergences.
  • Rival traditions of law, burial, oath, and sorcery hardened into political identities.
  • Trade linked regions that still possessed no single realm-wide government.

docs.title: The Great Tribulation
docs.text:
The final centuries produced overlapping disasters rather than one clean war.

  • Early human kingdoms fought with poorly constrained magic.
  • The Storm Knights rose, divided, and were destroyed.
  • The dead later associated with Blackwater Bog accumulated in wars no surviving record fully explains.
  • The enormous burial complexes of The Urmong Barrows received soldiers, nobles, healers, weapons, and dangerous sealed remnants.
  • Dwarven wealth and secrecy deepened after The Great Betrayal.
  • The Scattering drove the surviving Khaz’armok houses toward The Glimmering Expanse.
  • Delves were sealed, abandoned, lost, or cut off from one another.
  • Elven populations withdrew from open political life.
  • Roads failed, fields reverted to wilderness, and surviving settlements became isolated.

By the end of the Second Age, Saros contained people but no surviving network of human states. It was a land of hidden communities, ruined strongholds, scattered villages, and fragments of older knowledge.

docs.title: 0–120 AA — The Years of Gathering
docs.text:
Caelum’s wish brought approximately 900–1,000 Wanderers from Mystara. They gradually encountered another 6,000–10,000 Sarosians living in isolated communities.

Caelum found a land without functioning nations, not a land without people.

The survivors included:

  • Isolated farming clans
  • Hidden forest communities
  • Shepherd and herding groups
  • Monasteries preserving fragments of old knowledge
  • Refugees inside ruined fortresses
  • Fishing villages with little contact beyond their own bays
  • Families sheltering near Storm Knight tombs
  • Dwarves living outside sealed delves
  • Human communities that had forgotten the names of earlier kingdoms

docs.title: Major Developments
docs.text:
• The Wanderers established fortified camps near reliable water and sheltered coasts.
  • Native crops were combined with imported agricultural methods.
  • Old roads were cleared in short, defensible sections.
  • Goslow began as a landing, fishing settlement, and supply concentration near Bishop’s Bay.
  • Caelum negotiated, absorbed, allied with, and sometimes displaced existing communities.
  • Early arguments asked whether the newcomers were rescuers, conquerors, refugees, or invaders.
  • Mixed settlements developed shared law faster than they developed a shared identity.
  • Explorers vanished into old forests, delves, and ruins at a rate that discouraged rapid expansion.

docs.title: Population
docs.text:
• At Arrival: approximately 8,000–10,000 known people, including newcomers and discovered survivors
  • By 120 AA: approximately 10,000–13,000

The earliest records are household lists and ration counts, not censuses.

docs.title: 120–350 AA — The Chartering
docs.text: Stable towns and local governments appeared. Caelum’s influence spread along roads, rivers, ports, and negotiated charters rather than through complete control of the land between them.

docs.title: Major Developments
docs.text:
• Goslow received its first durable walls and harbor rules.
  • Port Quartz became a permanent ferry and transfer point.
  • Kylor supplied timber, pitch, charcoal, boats, and building material.
  • Skaggerty and similar crossroads communities became grain markets protected by palisades.
  • Early market towns received written charters recognizing local offices and obligations.
  • Standard coin weights and measures began to spread.
  • The earliest durable guilds formed around merchants, builders, sailors, and craftspeople.
  • Native Sarosian families entered the new civic and commercial elite.
  • Predecessor companies of The Aegis Legion guarded roads, stores, and expeditions.
  • Formal contact with Thar’um holds reopened limited dwarven trade.
  • Local law remained more important than distant proclamations outside the principal routes.

docs.title: Population
docs.text:
• Around 200 AA: 13,000–17,000
  • By 350 AA: approximately 22,000–30,000

Growth came from safer harvests, the joining of previously uncounted communities, and movement toward defended settlements as much as from births.

docs.title: 350–600 AA — The Long Founding
docs.text: During the Long Founding, the political culture associated with modern Saros became dominant across the best-connected regions.

docs.title: Major Developments
docs.text:
• The High Road linked Goslow to the royal height above Bishop’s Bay.
  • Pyrris and the early works of The Radiant Citadel became the royal and administrative center.
  • Crown road, river, ferry, and salvage laws took recognizable form.
  • Southern expeditions founded new settlements or absorbed older ones into the charter network.
  • Albyrt and Isoltide grew around the twin-lake trade.
  • Soryn’s Crossing, Trystn, and other freight centers became permanent market towns.
  • Guilds accumulated multigenerational records, privileges, and rivalries.
  • Commanders, towns, and merchants began the first major disputes over the limits of emergency authority.
  • Saros reused Second Age walls, cisterns, bridges, tomb roads, and foundations whenever repair was easier than new construction.
  • Dwarven and elven knowledge entered trade selectively and remained largely controlled by its keepers.

docs.title: Caelum’s End, about 600 AA
docs.text:
Near the close of this period, Caelum and Amara took their former pupil Silas Voss to the frozen northern peak now called Caelum’s End. It was their final attempt to turn him away from evil.

  • Caelum, Amara, and Silas were present.
  • No one but Amara witnessed the end.
  • Caelum and Silas both went over the edge into the northern sea.
  • Amara returned alone.
  • Caelum did not return.
  • Neither man has been reliably seen since, and the fate of both remains unknown.
  • Amara assumed Caelum’s throne in Pyrris.

docs.title: Population
docs.text: • By 600 AA: approximately 35,000–50,000

docs.title: 600–1,000 AA — The Early Amaran Peace
docs.text: Amara’s early reign transformed a founder’s network into a durable realm. “Peace” is relative: roads remained dangerous, towns fought, and entire districts could still disappear. The period was peaceful compared with what came before it.

docs.title: Major Developments
docs.text:
• The Aegis Legion became the principal realm-wide military institution.
  • The Crown recognized and regularized municipal charters.
  • The Queen’s Council became the permanent machinery of finance, law, diplomacy, intelligence, military policy, and magical oversight.
  • Roads, bridges, mile markers, and signal systems were standardized along principal routes.
  • The southern lake cities became major population and trade centers.
  • Rore repeatedly resisted royal authority and developed its independent civic traditions.
  • The Black Circle spread as a decentralized answer to concentrated power and dangerous neglected places.
  • Guilds expanded between cities and began enforcing rules through reputation as well as law.
  • Monasteries, temples, and archives copied older records before more originals were lost.
  • Frontier settlements grew around forts, mines, ferries, forests, and reclaimed farmland.

docs.title: Population
docs.text:
• Around 900 AA: approximately 80,000–100,000
  • By 1,000 AA: approximately 105,000–125,000

Population rose unevenly. Several local booms ended in plague, failed harvest, magical disaster, or abandonment.

docs.title: 1,000–1,300 AA — The High Peace
docs.text: Most institutions considered “old” in modern daily life took their present form during the High Peace.

docs.title: Major Developments
docs.text:
• Goslow reached true city size and became the realm’s commercial heart.
  • Merchant houses became multigenerational institutions.
  • Guild halls, temples, stone walls, mills, quays, courts, and civic monuments were built or rebuilt.
  • The Legion established much of its present fortress and patrol network.
  • Long-distance trade became routine enough for ordinary people to plan lives around it.
  • The Gambler’s Guild linked its chartered halls through the Bank of Saros.
  • Port Quartz grew wealthy through ferries, storage, salvage, and northern goods.
  • Lilya expanded beneath The Silvervein Summits.
  • Mysha became known for timber and halfling-grown Smoke Leaf.
  • Exploration reclaimed some old sites as mines, monasteries, keeps, or roads.
  • Other expeditions opened dangers that required the same sites to be sealed again.
  • Crown law became predictable on the major roads without ever making the wilderness between them safe.

docs.title: Population
docs.text:
• Around 1,200 AA: approximately 190,000–220,000
  • By 1,300 AA: approximately 240,000–270,000

docs.title: 1,300 AA–Present — The Fraying Peace
docs.text: The system stopped expanding consistently and began spending more effort preserving what already existed.

docs.title: Major Developments
docs.text:
• Roads beyond the principal routes deteriorated.
  • Legion commanders assumed increasing local authority under claims of emergency.
  • Pirates and brigands became bolder as patrol coverage thinned.
  • Guilds withheld taxes, hired private guards, and enforced their own contracts.
  • The Black Circle accused the Council and Legion of abandoning old protections while expanding control.
  • Several settlements disappeared, failed, or became isolated.
  • Dangerous magic resurfaced in regions assumed to be stable.
  • The northern wilderness became harder to reach and less reliably mapped.
  • Amara withdrew increasingly from ordinary government.
  • Her disappearance transformed a slow institutional decline into an open crisis of legitimacy.

docs.title: Population
docs.text:
• Present estimate: approximately 300,000
  • Plausible range: 280,000–320,000
  • Official Council count: 260,000–275,000

The Third Age has not officially ended. Later historians may decide that Amara’s disappearance marked the beginning of a Fourth Age.

docs.title: How Modern Saros Is Settled
docs.text:
Saros practices nucleated settlement. People cluster behind walls, palisades, watch posts, and old stone rather than living evenly across the countryside.

A typical agricultural community has:

  • 200–500 residents
  • A palisade or repaired older wall
  • A communal granary
  • A watchtower, bell, or signal fire
  • Fields extending one or two miles from shelter
  • A temple, shrine, or local ward
  • A militia of 20–60 adults
  • One maintained road toward a market town

Farmers leave the walls to work during daylight and return before dark. Isolated farms exist, but they are risky and often short-lived.

docs.title: Present Distribution
docs.text:
The currently named settlements in Major Cities, Towns, and Ports account for approximately 73,600 permanent residents, including the Thar’um stronghold of Dun Karag. The rest live in places too small, hidden, mobile, contested, or numerous for the continental map.

Settlement Pattern Approximate Population Major named settlements and strongholds 73,600 Secondary market towns and fortified towns 42,000 Independent villages, farms, and agricultural holds 154,400 Hidden enclaves, delves, pirate ports, nomads, islands, and remote camps 30,000 Working total 300,000

These numbers are deliberately approximate. Seasonal workers, sailors, soldiers, pilgrims, caravans, refugees, and uncounted communities constantly blur the categories.

docs.title: Why Goslow Dominates
docs.text:
Goslow supports about 14,000 permanent residents, making it the largest city in Saros.

It can hold that population because:

  • Many central buildings have two floors.
  • Families live above workshops and businesses.
  • Several buildings contain multiple households.
  • Sailors and laborers use boarding houses.
  • Wealthier properties include servants and extended families.
  • Warehouses and civic buildings occupy much of the waterfront.
  • Its harbor gathers food and material from a broad trade network.

Goslow is not surrounded by one enormous rural district. It consumes the output of many independent communities:

  • Grain from Skaggerty’s wider agricultural belt, Trystn, and southern routes
  • Fresh and preserved seafood from Bishop’s Bay, Kylor, and coastal settlements
  • Timber, pitch, and charcoal from Kylor
  • Northern goods through Port Quartz
  • Livestock driven along guarded roads
  • Coastal shipments from southern Saros
  • Royal supply contracts bound for Pyrris

Its ordinary daytime population may reach 15,000–17,000. Fairs, festivals, or fleet gatherings can push the number higher.

The canonical route, freight, food-demand, and settlement-distance model is maintained in Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population.

docs.title: Why Pyrris Is Called a City
docs.text:
Pyrris has only about 1,100 permanent residents. It is a city by charter, history, and function rather than size.

Its population chiefly supports:

  • The Citadel household and maintenance works
  • Legion guards and officers
  • Scribes, judges, clerks, and royal officials
  • Diplomats and council attendants
  • Priests, scholars, and magical specialists
  • Inns, stables, licensed merchants, and dependent families

Large cisterns, royal granaries, the High Road, and lifting works above Bishop’s Bay make the fortress-city possible. Hearings, festivals, and crises can temporarily raise its population to 2,000–3,000.

docs.title: Why Fourteen Centuries Did Not Fill the Map
docs.text:
Fourteen centuries allowed Saros to develop cities, guilds, regional identities, legal traditions, architectural layers, grudges, and repeated cycles of prosperity. It did not produce uninterrupted expansion.

Growth repeatedly strikes limits:

  • Safe farmland clusters around protected settlements.
  • Monsters recolonize abandoned territory.
  • Old magical contamination ruins promising regions.
  • Major roads require constant patrol and repair.
  • Sea and river trade face piracy, weather, and creatures.
  • Plague, famine, war, and monster incursions erase local population booms.
  • Dwarven and elven knowledge is deliberately controlled.
  • Guilds hoard technical knowledge that protects their influence.
  • Magic replaces some technologies without becoming broadly available.
  • Recovered ancient structures are easier to reuse than new infrastructure is to build.
  • Amara’s extremely long reign encouraged legal and technical conservatism.
  • The Council often preferred a manageable chain of towns over uncontrolled settlement.

A modern city therefore contains layers rather than steady progress: Second Age foundations, Third Age sewers, a five-hundred-year-old wall, a newly rebuilt guildhall, and homes standing over an unexplored ruin.

docs.title: The Six-Century Question
docs.text:
If Caelum arrived around 0 AA and fell at Caelum’s End around 600 AA, the human founder lived for roughly six centuries after the Arrival.

Sarosian scholars offer several explanations:

  • The wish bound Caelum’s life to the survival of the Wanderers.
  • He gave up the source of immortality but retained centuries already taken from time.
  • Passage from Mystara altered time for some original arrivals.
  • A powerful artifact sustained him until it was lost or surrendered.
  • Early chroniclers combined more than one event under a single reign.

The strongest court tradition says the wish would not release Caelum until his people were secure. In that reading, his fall marks the moment the refugee colony became Amara’s kingdom.

No surviving public record proves the explanation. The extraordinary lifespan is established history; its cause remains lore, faith, and political argument.

docs.title: Working Canon Summary
docs.text:
• Caelum’s wish brought nearly one thousand Wanderers to Saros about fourteen centuries ago.
  • They found no surviving open kingdoms, but they did find several thousand Sarosians in isolated communities.
  • The combined population grew through alliance, consolidation, migration, and ordinary generations.
  • Modern Saros has roughly 300,000 inhabitants.
  • Goslow, at about 14,000, is its largest city and commercial center.
  • Pyrris, at about 1,100, is a fortress-capital sustained by Goslow and royal infrastructure.
  • About three quarters of Sarosians live outside the named map settlements.
  • Civilization survives as defended concentrations connected by narrow roads through much older wilderness.

docs.title: The Great Betrayal
docs.text: The Great Betrayal was the civil war that shattered the Khaz’armok and drove its surviving houses toward The Glimmering Expanse.

docs.title: The Gem
docs.text:
After The Wandering, the leading Khaz’armok houses were closely allied and their elders were remembered as personal friends. Some traditions claim the houses had inherited custody of a discovery first made by the older Khaz’um.

That relationship ended over what later stories call the finest gem ever found in Saros. Fragmentary accounts call it the Deep Jewel, but do not agree whether it was a portable stone, an exposed crystal face, an entire chamber, or a name for something less easily described.

Several houses claimed the right to possess it. The two largest coalitions became so distinct during the dispute that later outsiders mistook them for separate clans; old human records call one side the Khaz’dar.

docs.title: The Blood Feud
docs.text:
Negotiation collapsed into violence.

The dispute became a large war whose memory still survives in dwarven clan identity.

The irony repeated in nearly every version is that neither side kept control of the gem.

Later histories usually say it was stolen. Dwarven versions are less certain: the chamber may have been sealed, its approaches destroyed, its location erased, or its surviving custodians killed before they could pass on the route.

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
The feud destroyed or divided most known Khaz’armok holds. Stone-shapers, dune-breakers, and sand guides were driven toward The Glimmering Expanse during The Scattering, where their later fate became one of Saros’s great dwarven mysteries.

Modern dwarven histories treat Khaz’dar as an obsolete name for one belligerent tradition, not as a surviving fourth clan.

docs.title: The Scattering
docs.text:
The Scattering is the name given to the flight and dispersal of the surviving Khaz’armok houses after The Great Betrayal.

It is distinct from The Wandering. The Wandering was the earlier expansion of the united Khaz’um and the formation of the later Dwarven Clans. The Scattering was a forced diaspora caused by civil war, ruined holds, broken alliances, and the loss of safe deep roads.

Most accounts send the surviving houses toward The Glimmering Expanse. Whether they died there, passed through it, or established hidden settlements remains one of Saros’s great dwarven mysteries.

docs.title: The Spring Harvest Festival
docs.text:
Wonderful foods, lavish entertainment, and games of all sorts are plentiful during The Festival. The Spring Harvest is celebrated by most civilized peoples of Saros in their own ways, but the largest celebration is held annually at the Capitol in Pyrris.

A long standing tradition, predating even Queen Amara’s rule, it’s a busy time filled with anticipation, as ripened fruits are being collected and new seeds are planted with hopes of a bountiful fall harvest. Spring rains nourish the young plants, and farmers must be vigilant in protecting their crops from pests and disease. While also inventorying and delivering their goods to the Festival.

docs.title: The Wandering
docs.text: The Wandering is the traditional name for the era when the earliest remembered dwarves, the Khaz’um, spread outward to chart and settle the deeper places of Saros.

docs.title: Expansion
docs.text:
Dwarven explorers discovered powerful Fey-Lines and rich mineral regions throughout the mountains.

Families and expedition groups began settling near the most promising sites.

Over generations, those settlements developed distinct customs, specialties, and identities.

The old Khaz’um identity gradually gave way to the Dwarven Clans remembered today.

docs.title: Delves
docs.text:
The Wandering saw the foundation of many early Delves.

At first, cooperation between settlements was common. Dwarven builders, miners, gem-workers, and surveyors shared knowledge across large distances.

That unity weakened as individual clans grew wealthy and protective of their discoveries.

The period of broad cooperation ended most dramatically with The Great Betrayal.

The later flight of the surviving Khaz’armok is called The Scattering. It should not be confused with the Wandering: one was an age of expansion and settlement, while the other was a forced diaspora after civil war.

docs.title: Grave Asters
docs.text: Grave Asters are pale, star-shaped flowers that thrive in cool soil around old burial grounds, ruined chapels, and stone that has sheltered the dead.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
Across Saros, mourners leave grave asters at tombs as a promise that the deceased will be remembered without being called back. Petals are also dried for funeral incense, mourning sachets, and mild sleeping draughts.

The flowers are not poisonous, but concentrated pollen can make a breathing creature calm, drowsy, and unusually receptive to dreams.

docs.title: Folklore
docs.text: Healthy grave asters are sometimes taken as evidence that a grave is quiet. Sudden blackening, blooming out of season, or flowers turning toward a living visitor are treated as warnings that something beneath the earth remains unsettled.

docs.title: Sacred Mushrooms
docs.text:
Sacred mushrooms are a broad name used for several rare fungi employed in certain Sarosian divination practices.

The preparations are not ordinary food and are usually handled by experienced sages, priests, herbalists, or ritual specialists.

Ostalda of Temple of Torm is known for years of divinatory use.

Her skin has developed a distinctive blue cast that locals attribute to repeated exposure.

Different traditions disagree over whether the mushrooms reveal genuine prophecy, heighten sensitivity to Fey-Lines, or simply place the mind in a state where meaningful patterns can be recognized.

docs.title: Fey-Lines
docs.text:
Fey-Lines are loosely connected streams of magical energy believed to flow beneath and through Saros.

They are not visible like ordinary rivers, but their effects can sometimes be recognized in unusually vigorous life, strange magical behavior, old ruins, or materials formed near powerful convergences.

docs.title: Convergences
docs.text:
Where several lines meet, magical energy becomes significantly stronger.

These convergences shaped the development of older civilizations.

docs.title: Elven Use
docs.text:
Elven traditions used fey-line power to:

  • Encourage extraordinary plant growth
  • Sustain hidden woodland domains
  • Conceal settlements
  • Strengthen living landscapes

docs.title: Dwarven Use
docs.text:
The Dwarven Clans established many Delves near known convergences.

They used the energy to support deep construction, magical craft, and the extraction of rare materials such as Fey-stone.

docs.title: Modern Understanding
docs.text:
Modern scholars can recognize some fey-line effects but do not possess a complete map of the network.

Old routes may weaken, shift, or behave differently after magical disasters.

Because fey-lines connect distant places, damage at one convergence can sometimes produce effects far from the obvious source.

docs.title: Fey-stone
docs.text:
Fey-stone is a rare dull-grey material found near powerful convergences of Fey-Lines.

In its raw state it can look unimpressive: a dense, malleable stone with little of the sparkle associated with ordinary precious gems.

Its value appears only when someone knows how to work it.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Properly prepared Fey-stone can accept magical properties with unusual stability.

It has been used in:

  • Weapons
  • Armor
  • Ritual tools
  • Magical fittings
  • Prosthetics
  • Old dwarven machinery

docs.title: Working Fey-stone
docs.text:
The material is notoriously difficult to forge or shape without ruining its magical potential.

Bedford of Bedford’s Forge in Goslow is one of the few living craftspeople publicly known to work it reliably.

Older dwarven traditions, especially those associated with the Thar’um, are believed to understand the material far better than most modern Sarosians.

docs.title: Golden Grouper
docs.text:
The Golden Grouper is one of the better-known sailor stories of Bishop’s Bay.

Legend describes an immense grouper, sometimes said to be as large as a whale, whose scales or flesh shine like worked gold.

docs.title: Origin of the Story
docs.text:
The most popular version claims the creature began as an ordinary goldfish belonging to a mad alchemist.

Something went wrong—or exactly right—with an experiment involving growth and transmutation.

The fish escaped, continued growing, and eventually became the monster of the modern tale.

docs.title: Sightings
docs.text:
No two descriptions agree on its exact size.

Sailors have blamed the Grouper for:

  • Missing nets
  • Damaged small boats
  • Enormous shadows below the water
  • Schools of fish suddenly fleeing an area
  • Gold-colored flashes far below the surface

Mirken Stanton is famously obsessed with finding it and insists the creature is real.

docs.title: Storm Knights
docs.text:
The Storm Knights were one of the great human powers of the Second Age.

Their surviving ruins suggest a civilization far more technically and magically sophisticated than most people expect from early Sarosian humanity.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Legends credit the Storm Knights with mastery of:

  • Esoteric fey-line magic
  • Fortification
  • Strange mental or psionic disciplines
  • Long-distance roads and outposts
  • Tombs and protective complexes

How much of that reputation is accurate remains uncertain.

docs.title: Ruins
docs.text:
Storm Knight structures appear throughout Saros, often in places where no modern settlement could easily support such construction.

Some have become:

  • Temples
  • Forts
  • Tombs
  • Dungeons
  • Roadside ruins
  • Refuges used by later peoples

Veiled Archive is one surviving complex associated with them.

docs.title: Fall
docs.text:
No complete account explains how the Storm Knights ended.

Their decline is tied broadly to the wars and political collapse remembered as the Great Tribulation.

docs.title: The Great Sphinx
docs.text:
The Great Sphinx is one of the enduring legends of The Glimmering Expanse.

The creature is said to dwell somewhere deep within the glass desert, far beyond routes most travelers can survive.

docs.title: The Wish
docs.text:
Stories claim the Sphinx can grant a wish.

Unlike the legends surrounding a multi-chromatic dragon, the Sphinx supposedly chooses according to character rather than opportunity.

Only someone it judges pure of heart is allowed to receive the gift.

What the Sphinx considers pure is never explained consistently.

docs.title: The Voices
docs.text:
The strangest repeated detail is its speech.

The Sphinx is said to use a different voice with every sentence.

Witnesses in old stories describe hearing:

  • A child
  • An old woman
  • A soldier
  • A banshee
  • A loved one
  • Their own voice

Whether the effect is illusion, prophecy, mind-reading, or storytelling embellishment is unknown.

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
No widely accepted expedition record confirms the Sphinx exists.

That has never stopped people from searching.

docs.title: Caelum
docs.text: Caelum was a powerful human wizard from Mystara and the figure whose desperate wish began the modern history of Saros.

docs.title: The Wish
docs.text:
Facing the destruction of his people, Caelum sought aid beyond anything ordinary magic could provide.

Tradition says he used Contact Higher Plane and reached a power identified in later accounts as Bahamut.

Caelum asked for his remaining people to be carried somewhere they could survive.

Nearly one thousand beings were transported to Saros.

Different traditions disagree about the exact price of the wish. One enduring account claims Caelum surrendered an unnatural immortality or the means of preserving it in exchange for his people’s safety.

docs.title: King Caelum
docs.text:
Caelum became the central political figure of the newly arrived people.

His reputation combines:

  • Powerful wizard
  • Refugee leader
  • Founder
  • King
  • Explorer
  • Husband of Queen Amara

He lived for centuries after the Arrival, an extraordinary lifespan even by magical standards.

docs.title: Caelum’s End
docs.text:
Roughly eight hundred years ago, Caelum and Queen Amara brought Silas Voss to the northernmost foot-navigable point of Saros for one final attempt to turn their former pupil away from evil.

Only Amara witnessed the end. Caelum and Silas both went over the frozen edge into the sea below.

Caelum did not return. Silas eventually did.

Amara returned alone to Pyrris, where she assumed her husband’s throne.

The place became known as Caelum’s End.

What caused the fall, what Caelum intended, and what Amara saw remain among the great unanswered questions of Sarosian history.

docs.title: Edric Vane
docs.text:
Edric Vane led one of the best-known expeditions from Port Quartz toward The Masys Mountains centuries ago.

Later retellings turned him into an uncomplicated frontier hero. The surviving records tell a harsher story.

Edric departed with approximately sixty people.

Seven returned.

docs.title: The Expedition
docs.text:
The expedition charted:

  • Western river crossings
  • Seasonal flood zones
  • Mountain approaches
  • Old ruins and abandoned works
  • Areas where pack animals could still be moved
  • Places where the terrain forced the party to turn back

Several journal pages are missing, but nothing in the surviving record describes Rom or the moving hill found in recent folklore.

Those legends would not arise for centuries.

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text:
Edric’s records remain useful because the geography has changed less than the stories.

His descendant Hesta Vane protects the surviving documents in the Vane Archive and dislikes anyone who treats the expedition’s losses as romantic scenery.

docs.title: Rom The Wizard
docs.text:
Legends tell of an old and exceedingly strange wizard called Rom who has lived somewhere near the southern reaches of The Masys Mountains for roughly eighty years.

The stories are unusually inconsistent even by Sarosian standards. Rom is described as a hermit, a prophet, a dangerous fool, an ancient magical scholar, and occasionally as someone who answers questions before they are asked.

One detail appears in several versions of the tale: Rom’s home does not remain in one place. Some travelers call it a moving hill; others insist the hill bears gardens and lanterns.

docs.title: The Age of the Legend
docs.text:
There are no centuries-old accounts of Rom or a moving hill in the Masys region.

Old expedition journals such as those of Edric Vane describe the terrain, rivers, mountain approaches, and dangers of the northwest but contain nothing resembling a giant snail or moving hill.

The first credible Rom stories begin only within the last eight decades.

docs.title: Port Quartz Stories
docs.text:
In Port Quartz, Rom remains a frontier legend. Most people have never met anyone who can honestly claim to have seen him.

People who have traveled far beyond Westwater Ferry sometimes tell of:

  • Strange healthy clearings in otherwise sick forest
  • Impossible lights moving among the hills
  • A distant rounded shape that is gone by morning
  • Carefully placed stones bearing warnings no local scholar understands

None of those signs appear near Port Quartz itself.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text: Those who believe in Rom generally agree on one thing: if the magic of northern Saros is truly failing, he may be one of the few people strange enough to understand why.

docs.title: The Serpent King
docs.text:
The Serpent King was an ancient snake-man ruler whose underground domain once occupied part of the region south of modern Goslow.

Later stories describe him as a fair and generous king besieged by enemies on several sides.

docs.title: Obsession
docs.text:
Despite his reputation as a capable ruler, the Serpent King spent an enormous share of his wealth seeking immortality.

He ordered his court wizard, Xiximanter, to discover a reliable path to eternal life or a fountain of youth.

The search consumed years and resources.

docs.title: Death
docs.text:
The King died before Xiximanter completed his experiments.

His realm eventually collapsed and the underground city fell into ruin.

The site is now known as Tomb of The Serpent King.

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text: The irony of a ruler spending so much of his life trying not to die has made the Serpent King a favorite subject of priests, gamblers, and tavern philosophers throughout Goslow.

docs.title: Xiximanter
docs.text:
A centuries old Snake-Man Wizard… Xiximanter was left in his laboratory by The Serpent King to work on his time experiments, and unbeknownst to himself, succeeded. When he was found by a party of adventurers, it so happened that what seemed like a few days to him was actually hundreds of years in Saros. While he worked, his civilization crumbled around him and his once great culture has been left to history.

He currently lives in the Tomb of The Serpent King and is very friendly to most bipeds, usually willing to talk and negotiate deals if anyone seeks his knowledge of time manipulation. He absolutely HATES goblins and will become enraged at the sight of one unbound.

docs.title: Fall Casks
docs.text:
Fall casks are heavily reinforced cargo barrels used to send durable goods from the high basin around Lake of Lament down the otherwise unnavigable waterfall feeding the river toward Port Quartz.

No ship can climb the cataract. A properly built cask can survive going over it.

The practice is dangerous, expensive, and inefficient compared with a road caravan, but it allows small quantities of dense or valuable cargo from the Lilya region to move south without first traveling through Trystn.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
A proper fall cask is usually:

  • Built from thick, slightly flexible timber
  • Bound with multiple iron hoops
  • Sealed internally with pitch and wax
  • Packed tightly with straw, wool, sawdust, cloth, or fitted wooden braces
  • Marked with a registered owner or sender brand
  • Fitted with a durable consignment plate or waxed shipping tag
  • Balanced so that it floats in a predictable orientation after the fall

The best cooperages charge heavily because a poor cask may arrive as scattered firewood.

docs.title: Common Cargo
docs.text:
Fall casks are best suited for:

  • Metal ingots
  • Ore samples
  • Durable tools
  • Stone carvings
  • Pigments and mineral salts
  • Sealed alchemical materials
  • Dried herbs
  • Small quantities of valuable, shock-resistant goods

People, animals, glassware, ordinary food cargo, and delicate manufactured goods generally travel by road.

docs.title: Recovery at Port Quartz
docs.text:
Catch crews at Cataract Yard use chain booms, hooks, boats, winches, and recovery cranes to pull surviving casks from the river.

A recovered cask is logged before it is opened or released.

The recovery crew is entitled to a standard salvage and handling fee even when the rightful owner is known.

docs.title: Salvage and Claim Law
docs.text: The Mooring Council maintains strict claim rules because ownership disputes are nearly as common as broken casks.

docs.title: Registered cask with a living owner or named recipient
docs.text: The cask remains the property of the registered owner or named consignee. It is released after identity, registration, recovery fees, and applicable customs are settled.

docs.title: Registered sender is deceased or missing
docs.text:
A named recipient still has the strongest claim.

If there is no named recipient, an acknowledged estate representative, business partner with documented authority, or insurer may submit a claim.

docs.title: Damaged mark or disputed ownership
docs.text:
The cask is moved into the claim yard at Cataract Yard.

Claimants must produce records strong enough for the salvage clerk or Mooring Council to recognize a lawful interest.

docs.title: Unmarked or genuinely unclaimed cask
docs.text:
The town holds the cask for thirty days.

During that period it may not be sold, stripped, or privately opened except under a recognized safety exception.

If no valid claim is established by the end of the period, the Mooring Council may auction the cargo. Recovery fees and town charges are paid first.

docs.title: Altering a brand
docs.text: Removing, burning over, or changing a registered cask mark is treated as deliberate cargo theft and is punished much more severely than ordinary scavenging.

docs.title: Opening a Held Cask
docs.text:
A held cask is normally kept sealed.

The civic authorities may order a supervised opening when there is a credible reason to believe the contents are:

  • Leaking
  • Dangerous
  • Perishable in a way that threatens nearby cargo
  • Magical and unstable
  • Evidence in a serious crime
  • Falsely presented as military or civic property

A disputed military claim does not automatically transfer ownership to The Aegis Legion. Port Quartz’s charter requires a lawful seizure, recognized emergency, or agreement with the Mooring Council.

docs.title: Local Saying
docs.text: “The fall decides what reaches Quartz. The Council decides whose it is.”

docs.title: Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population
docs.text:
This note is the canonical working source for travel, trade routes, settlement spacing, and population in Saros. Route estimates should be revised here first and then reflected in the relevant settlement notes.

The familiar continental map is not a modern survey. The version displayed in The Toad was commissioned by Perla Mudridge from an artist who did not possess precise measurements of the entire land.

For game purposes, the map is:

  • Reliable in general direction
  • Useful for regional distance
  • Good enough to plan journeys
  • Not accurate enough to measure every river bend, coastline, cliff, or road mathematically

Working map scale: one small hex is approximately 5 miles across; one large hex, composed of smaller hexes, is approximately 30 miles across.

docs.title: Recommended Size of Saros
docs.text:
Measure Working Estimate Broadest east-to-west span ~220–260 miles Greatest north-to-south span ~330–380 miles Approximate land area ~45,000–60,000 square miles Small hex ~5 miles Large hex ~30 miles Typical mounted road day ~1 large hex

This makes Saros a large island or small continental fragment. It is large enough for neighboring towns to be days apart and for regional economies to develop distinct identities. It is small enough for trade to circulate, important people to become known across the realm, and a campaign to cross much of the known world.

docs.title: Cartographic Error Allowance
docs.text: Allow roughly ±15–20% when measuring directly from the map. Winding roads, river bends, mountain passes, symbolic settlement placement, distorted coastlines, abandoned roads, and ordinary artistic error all affect the result.

docs.title: The Most Important Geographic Rule
docs.text:
Northern Saros is divided by enormous rivers that function more like inland seas than ordinary streams.

Goslow, Pyrris, Kylor, Skaggerty, and much of the country northwest of Skaggerty occupy a western pocket bounded by huge waterways.

To the northeast, the great river descending from The Masys Mountains blocks ordinary movement. To the southeast, another massive river divides the Goslow–Pyrris country from the region of Port Quartz.

These waterways are too broad, deep, violent, or strategically difficult for ordinary bridges. Obscure crossings may be known to explorers, smugglers, monsters, older civilizations, or travelers using magic, but they are not commercial roads.

docs.title: Goslow to Port Quartz
docs.text:
There is no normal safe overland road between Goslow and Port Quartz.

The principal civilized route is by ship. A vessel:

  1. Leaves Goslow southward through Bishop’s Bay.
  2. Keeps clear of the guarded cliffside waters beneath Pyrris and the restricted waterline approach called Queen’s Gate.
  3. Turns northeast into the great river.
  4. Works upstream toward Port Quartz.

This is one of northern Saros’s most important trade arteries. Several vessels make some portion of the passage every week. Shipping is not merely convenient; it is necessary to the northern economy.

docs.text:
Draft animals consume cargo simply by existing. Water is usually obtained along a route; feed requires pasture, roadside fodder, purchased hay, grain depots, inns, villages, or carried supplies.

docs.title: Skaggerty to Goslow
docs.text: The town of Skaggerty and its wider belt of fortified farms and villages form one of the cleanest grain corridors in the western pocket. The town is a gathering, milling, weighing, storage, and wagon-dispatch center rather than the sole producer of every load bearing its name.

docs.title: Feeding Goslow
docs.text:
Goslow does not live on imported grain alone. Its staple network combines:

  • Grain, beans, roots, vegetables, and livestock from nearby agriculture and Skaggerty’s farm belt
  • Fresh, smoked, salted, and preserved seafood from Bishop’s Bay and neighboring coasts
  • Fish and preserved goods from Kylor
  • Coastal shipments from southern Saros
  • Imports, specialty food, and emergency stores moving through its harbor

The bay’s fisheries reduce the city’s dependence on any single grain harvest. Grain remains strategically important for bread, porridge, brewing, animal feed, ship provisions, and the supply of Pyrris.

docs.title: Goslow to Pyrris
docs.text: Every wagon supplying Pyrris must climb The High Road. The capital receives grain, preserved seafood, livestock products, timber, and manufactured goods through Goslow. This expensive supply line helps keep the capital small.

docs.title: Port Quartz to Trystn to Lilya
docs.text: Feed grain, food, mine timbers, tools, and other supplies move inland. Ore and finished mineral goods travel in the opposite direction. The cost of feeding draft animals is built into every pound of Lilyan ore reaching Port Quartz.

docs.title: Water Is the Backbone of Trade
docs.text:
The practical commercial map is built around:

  • Bishop’s Bay
  • The Goslow–Port Quartz shipping route
  • The rivers connected to Port Quartz
  • The lake crossing between Albyrt and Isoltide
  • Southern river traffic through Soryn’s Crossing
  • Eastern coastal routes through Rore and Ari
  • Military sea lanes around Grymswatch and Karastos

This explains why pirates remain politically important and why a modest port can be strategically powerful.

docs.title: Griffin Travel
docs.text:
Griffin Riders make the Aegis Legion strategically mobile without replacing ships or roads.

  • Ordinary movement: 70–100 miles/day
  • Emergency courier: 120–150 miles/day
  • Light cargo only
  • Weather, landing sites, food, rest, handlers, and specialized care still matter

Their greatest strategic advantage is the ability to ignore rivers. A griffin can cross in hours a barrier that forces a merchant into a multi-day shipping route. Their limited cargo and tremendous upkeep keep them from replacing boats carrying grain.

docs.title: Working Canon Summary
docs.text:
Saros uses a working scale of approximately 5 miles per small hex and 30 miles per large hex.

The known land is roughly 220–260 miles across and 330–380 miles north-to-south, but the familiar map is intentionally approximate.

Named settlements and strongholds contain about 73,600 people. The working total population is approximately 300,000.

Skaggerty is a 1,200-person agricultural market town serving a much larger belt of farms and fortified villages.

Goslow, Pyrris, Kylor, Skaggerty, and the western northern country are separated from Port Quartz by enormous rivers. There is no ordinary safe commercial road between Goslow and Port Quartz.

The normal Goslow–Port Quartz connection is a 70–90 mile water route.

Goslow is fed by grain and produce, but also by extensive seafood from Bishop’s Bay and neighboring coasts.

Saros should feel like fortified islands of civilization connected by roads, rivers, ports, ferries, and sea lanes through an older and more dangerous world.

docs.title: Smoke Leaf
docs.text:
Smoke Leaf is an aromatic cultivated plant grown throughout Saros. Its dried leaves and flowers are smoked, steeped into bitter tea, or baked into small confections for relaxation, pain relief, appetite, and convivial use.

Use is common among many classes and peoples. Customs vary by settlement, but most Sarosians treat smoke leaf much as they treat ale: ordinary in moderation, foolish before dangerous work, and a concern for local law only when it causes a public nuisance or neglect of duty.

docs.title: Trade
docs.text:
Nearly every agricultural region produces a local variety. Quality depends on seed, soil, curing, and the patience of the grower.

It is widely accepted that the finest smoke leaf comes from the halfling leaf farms around Mysha. Myshan growers guard family seed lines, cure their harvest in low cedar sheds, and sell named blends at prices that encourage counterfeiting elsewhere.

Smoke leaf travels well when kept dry. It is a common caravan good, tavern purchase, informal gift, and taxable luxury in towns that need easy revenue.

docs.title: Goslow
docs.text: Goslow is the largest city in the realm and the primary commercial concentration around Bishop’s Bay. Its connection to Pyrris through The High Road makes it the practical supply base of the Crown.

docs.title: Pyrris
docs.text: Pyrris is a capital by status rather than population. Most permanent residents support The Radiant Citadel, The Queen’s Council, court administration, diplomacy, or the Aegis Legion.

docs.title: Port Quartz
docs.text: Port Quartz controls an important ferry crossing and the transfer of goods among western, eastern, and northern routes. Its fall-cask trade is unique in Saros.

docs.title: Lilya
docs.text: Lilya exists because of the mineral wealth of The Silvervein Summits. Most ordinary freight moves south to Trystn.

docs.title: Kylor
docs.text: Kylor is a remote working port built around fishing and the timber trade.

docs.title: Dun Karag
docs.text: Dun Karag is the last permanent stronghold on the road to Caelum’s End. Its Thar’um wardens maintain and control the passage through The Masys Mountains.

docs.title: Rore
docs.text: Rore is independent, wealthy, and politically difficult for the Crown. Gambling, lending, trade, and a sophisticated black market support its economy.

docs.title: Southern Centers
docs.text:
Albyrt and Isoltide form the great twin-lake trade pair.

Soryn’s Crossing handles much of the south’s overland and river freight.

Ani watches the dangerous country around The Urmong Barrows.

Mysha is tied to logging and old halfling stories of Lake Runa.

Ari supports fishing, grain, and the smaller mining claims around Vy’Tungavor.

Brynk remains deliberately isolated despite its place on the map.

docs.title: Albyrt
docs.text: Albyrt is the larger western half of the twin cities on the great southern lake, facing Isoltide across the water. The two settlements grew around opposite ends of the lake’s trade and ferry routes and are culturally intertwined even when their councils disagree.

docs.title: Character
docs.text: Albyrt is sturdy, practical, and lake-oriented. Ferries, warehouses, grain yards, fish markets, and repair slips line the water. Travelers from the north often treat Albyrt and Isoltide as a single destination; residents are quick to explain why that is incorrect.

docs.title: Government
docs.text: A local charter council handles civic affairs under Mara Avelin, the current Lake Reeve. The Crown is recognized, but daily life is governed locally and the city’s relationship with Isoltide matters almost as much as its relationship with distant Pyrris.

docs.title: Trade and Economy
docs.text:
Albyrt lives on lake transport, fishing, grain, ferry service, warehousing, and goods moving between the western roads and the south.

Its position near routes toward the dangerous Urmong Barrows also supports outfitters, guides, and guards.

docs.title: Travel and Connections
docs.text:
Isoltide stands across the great southern lake. A ferry or lake boat crosses in less than a day, while going around takes about 2 days on foot, 2-3 days by heavy cart, or 1-2 days mounted.

The lake carries grain, fish, timber, livestock feed, stone, and passengers far more efficiently than the road. See Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population for the canonical route model.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: A lakeside wall, gatehouses, watch boats, and local militia protect the town. Patrols focus as much on the approaches from the Barrows as on ordinary crime.

  • Albyrt Grain Steps — terraced loading quays for grain and bulk goods
  • The Reed Crown — large lakeside inn serving merchants and ferry crews

docs.title: Albyrt Grain Steps
docs.text: The Albyrt Grain Steps are broad stone terraces descending toward the lake, designed so carts can unload grain directly into barges and ferries. On busy days the steps become one of the loudest places in Albyrt.

docs.title: Everyday Use
docs.text: Trade here follows the rhythms of arrivals and departures rather than a fixed modern schedule. Prices can change sharply when a caravan, fishing fleet, or shipment is late, and local information often moves between stalls faster than it reaches any official notice board.

docs.title: The Reed Crown
docs.text: The Reed Crown is a large lakeside inn in Albyrt favored by ferry crews and merchants. Its upper galleries look across the water toward Isoltide, and arguments about which twin city has the better view are encouraged because they sell drinks.

docs.title: Everyday Use
docs.text: The establishment serves as more than a place to drink or sleep. Travelers use it to hear road conditions, find temporary help, arrange meetings, and learn which local businesses are actually open to strangers.

docs.title: Westlake Ferry Hall
docs.text: Westlake Ferry Hall combines ferry offices, passenger records, and civic meeting rooms on the waterfront of Albyrt. Mara Avelin keeps her public office here. The hall’s bell tower signals dangerous lake weather and temporary ferry closures.

docs.title: Public Use
docs.text: Most residents encounter the building through ordinary civic business rather than ceremony. Notices, disputes, permits, records, and requests for local officials all pass through it, making the place a useful measure of what the settlement currently considers important.

docs.title: Mara Avelin
docs.text:
Mara Avelin is the current Lake Reeve of Albyrt, responsible for balancing ferry interests, grain merchants, shoreline households, and the constant civic comparison with Isoltide.

Mara is measured and patient in public, with the habit of asking for cargo numbers before entertaining grand political arguments. She came from a ferry-owning family and still knows the lake well enough to embarrass captains who exaggerate the weather.

She considers cooperation with Isoltide essential but dislikes any agreement that makes Albyrt appear secondary.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text: Mara is respected for treating lake traffic as infrastructure rather than ceremony. When weather turns bad, she is more likely to be found near the ferry office than at a formal council table.

docs.title: Ani
docs.text:
Ani is a fortified coastal town whose primary purpose is to protect settled southern Saros from dangers associated with The Urmong Barrows.

Fishing keeps the town fed, but defense defines its identity.

docs.title: Character
docs.text:
Ani is watchful. Gates close early, watch fires are maintained regardless of weather, and local children learn the alarm signals before they learn most prayers.

Travelers heading toward the Barrows are common. Travelers returning from them are memorable.

docs.title: Government
docs.text:
Ani operates under a March Charter that grants its defensive officers unusual local authority. Captain Lysa Dorn currently serves as March Warden.

The town cooperates closely with the Aegis Legion but retains its own militia and watch tradition.

docs.title: Travel and Connections
docs.text:
Ani is tied to southern Saros by coastal traffic and guarded roads, while Barrowgate controls the dangerous inland approach toward The Urmong Barrows. No dependable mileage for those expedition routes has yet been fixed.

See Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population for the current map scale and travel assumptions.

docs.title: Ani Watchhouse
docs.text: Ani Watchhouse is the headquarters of the town watch and militia under Captain Lysa Dorn. Signal gear, reserve weapons, and Barrowgate duty rosters are kept here.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The structure is part of the settlement’s ordinary defensive routine, not merely a wartime monument. Watch rotations, inspections, signal procedures, and emergency stores are maintained even during quiet seasons.

docs.title: Daily Routine
docs.text:
The Watchhouse keeps more than weapons. Patrol logs, signal codes, missing-person reports, and notes from travelers returning from The Urmong Barrows are stored here.

Captain Lysa Dorn expects every watch officer to know the current condition of Barrowgate and the inland warning posts before taking duty.

docs.title: Barrowgate
docs.text: Barrowgate is the heavily fortified inland gate of Ani, facing the roads and wild country toward The Urmong Barrows. Returning travelers are questioned here before being allowed into the town.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The structure is part of the settlement’s ordinary defensive routine, not merely a wartime monument. Watch rotations, inspections, signal procedures, and emergency stores are maintained even during quiet seasons.

docs.title: Returning from the Barrows
docs.text:
The gate watch pays special attention to people returning from The Urmong Barrows.

Travelers may be asked about missing companions, unusual wounds, objects recovered from tombs, and whether anything followed them.

The questions are not merely superstition; Ani has learned that some dangers arrive looking like exhausted adventurers.

docs.title: The Last Lantern
docs.text: The Last Lantern is the traditional gathering place for expeditions preparing to leave Ani toward The Urmong Barrows. Equipment changes hands constantly, and the walls carry memorial marks for groups that never returned.

docs.title: Everyday Use
docs.text: The establishment serves as more than a place to drink or sleep. Travelers use it to hear road conditions, find temporary help, arrange meetings, and learn which local businesses are actually open to strangers.

docs.title: Tradition
docs.text:
Groups heading toward The Urmong Barrows often leave a name, mark, or short note in the Lantern before departure.

Some are crossed out when the travelers return.

Others remain for years.

The practice is voluntary, but the collection has become an informal memorial and a useful record of who went into the Barrows.

docs.title: Captain Lysa Dorn
docs.text:
Captain Lysa Dorn is the March Warden of Ani, coordinating the town militia, coastal watch, and defensive preparations facing The Urmong Barrows.

She is not easily impressed by adventurers heading toward the Barrows. Ani sees a steady stream of confident people leave through Barrowgate, and far fewer return with the same confidence.

Lysa works closely with the Aegis Legion but considers Ani’s local watch traditions indispensable.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text: Lysa is not humorless, but most strangers meet her while discussing the Barrows, missing people, or defensive readiness. She has learned to ask adventurers about retreat plans before admiring their equipment.

docs.title: Ari
docs.text:
Ari is an eastern coastal town supported by fishing, nearby grain production, and small mining outposts working the lower country around Vy’Tungavor.

Its position makes it both a food producer and a staging point for prospectors moving toward the mountains.

docs.title: Character
docs.text: Ari feels divided between sea and mountain. Fish markets and grain warehouses line the low ground while miners, prospectors, and pack trains gather farther inland.

docs.title: Government
docs.text: A charter council led by Harlan Vey, the current Harbor Warden, balances fishing interests, farmers, merchants, and the owners of the smaller mining claims.

docs.title: Trade and Economy
docs.text:
• Fishing
  • Grain
  • Coastal shipping
  • Ore from small Vy’Tungavor outposts
  • Mining supplies
  • Food and equipment for prospectors

docs.title: Travel and Connections
docs.text:
Heavy trade with Rore normally follows the coast. A coastal trader can make the trip in about a day in favorable weather, while the overland journey takes roughly 4-5 days walking, 5-7 days by heavy wagon, or about 3 days mounted.

Inland pack routes lead toward the smaller claims and hatchling country of Vy’Tungavor, but no single dependable mileage describes those mountain journeys.

See Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population for the canonical route model.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Ari is fortified enough to resist raiders but cannot protect every mining camp in the mountains. Patrols concentrate on the road and harbor while outlying claims rely on hired guards.

docs.title: Places of Interest
docs.text:
• Ari Grain Quay — bulk grain and fish loading waterfront
  • Vytung Yard — pack trains and mining supply market
  • The Copper Gull — inn used by fishers and prospectors
