docs.title: Breakwater Registry
docs.text: The Breakwater Registry licenses and records specialized travel connected to Port Quartz.

docs.title: Registered Professions
docs.text:
The office maintains records for:

  • Ferry operators
  • Fall-cask recovery crews
  • Wilderness guides
  • Surveyors
  • Professional escorts
  • Certain river pilots

Travelers leaving established roads may also file a voluntary expedition declaration naming their route, expected return, and emergency contact.

docs.title: Public Board
docs.text:
The Registry posts:

  • Missing travelers
  • Closed ferry landings
  • River conditions
  • Dangerous wildlife
  • Suspected bandit activity
  • Guide availability
  • Recent warnings from surveyors

Hesta Vane treats the registry as a civic record rather than an automatic military intelligence file.

docs.title: Cataract Yard
docs.text:
Cataract Yard is the fall-cask recovery and salvage works of Port Quartz.

It sits along a heavily reinforced stretch of river equipped with chain booms, recovery hooks, cranes, winches, sorting platforms, cooperages, and guarded storage.

Goods deliberately sent over the great waterfall from the region around Lake of Lament are recovered here when they survive the journey.

See fall-cask for the full trade and ownership rules.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
Catch crews intercept surviving casks before they continue too far downstream.

Every recovered cask is:

  1. Hauled onto a numbered platform
  2. Recorded by brand and condition
  3. Checked for obvious leaks or hazards
  4. Assessed for recovery fees
  5. Released, forwarded, or moved into claim storage

docs.title: Claim Yard
docs.text:
The guarded claim yard holds casks whose ownership cannot immediately be resolved.

Common reasons include:

  • Damaged brands
  • Missing or deceased senders
  • Absent named recipients
  • Competing claims
  • Unmarked cargo
  • Suspicious or contradictory papers

Under Port Quartz law, genuinely unclaimed casks are normally held for thirty days before the Mooring Council can authorize auction.

A cask may be opened early under civic supervision when it is leaking, unstable, dangerous, or evidence in a serious dispute.

docs.title: Atmosphere
docs.text: After storms, Cataract Yard can become chaotic. Casks arrive mixed with branches, wreckage, dead animals, and whatever else the river has decided to surrender.

docs.title: Chainwatch
docs.text:
Chainwatch is a squat civic watch tower overlooking the busiest ferry landings of Port Quartz.

The local Chain Watch uses it to:

  • Observe river traffic
  • Coordinate signals with the White Quays
  • Announce ferry closures
  • Hold minor prisoners
  • Store unidentified river salvage
  • Respond to broken ferry lines

During an emergency, crews can use shore-mounted capstans and boats to draw a heavy warning chain across part of the lower harbor.

Chainwatch belongs to the town rather than the Aegis Legion.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The structure is part of the settlement’s ordinary defensive routine, not merely a wartime monument. Watch rotations, inspections, signal procedures, and emergency stores are maintained even during quiet seasons.

docs.title: Hall of Moorings
docs.text:
Hall of Moorings is the civic heart of Port Quartz and the usual workplace of Hesta Vane and the Mooring Council.

The broad, low stone building serves as town hall, customs office, civic court, archive office, and emergency command center.

docs.title: Main Chamber
docs.text:
The council table is said to have been built from timbers taken from one of Port Quartz’s earliest chartered ferries.

River charts, flood marks, ferry schedules, and memorial plaques cover the walls.

docs.title: Public Business
docs.text:
Travelers and merchants come here for:

  • Customs disputes
  • Salvage hearings
  • fall-cask claims
  • Ferry licenses
  • Major cargo declarations
  • Charter and property matters

The hall is deliberately civilian. Captain Serin Holt and the Aegis Legion may conduct official business here, but they do not command the building.

docs.title: Quartz Vaults
docs.text:
The Quartz Vaults are secure storage chambers cut into pale stone above the commercial waterfront of Port Quartz.

The upper chambers are leased to merchants for valuable or sensitive cargo.

Lower chambers are older than much of the present town, and several sealed doors have resisted generations of locksmiths.

docs.title: Civic Vaults
docs.text:
The Mooring Council maintains separate protected rooms for:

  • Confiscated cargo
  • Emergency grain
  • Important civic records
  • Hazardous salvage
  • Goods held during legal disputes

The vaults are watched closely because ownership arguments become much more expensive when the object in question can fit inside a locked room.

docs.title: Shrine of the Last Oar
docs.text:
The Shrine of the Last Oar is a small riverside sanctuary in Port Quartz dedicated to people lost upon the water.

Broken oars, carved names, recovered possessions, river stones, and family offerings fill the interior.

docs.title: Neutrality
docs.text:
The shrine does not distinguish between Crown sailors, pirates, merchants, ferrymen, Black Circle travelers, or ordinary dead.

That neutrality is respected strongly enough that even people who dislike one another may leave messages or arrange quiet meetings nearby.

“Grief has no faction.”

docs.title: Local Importance
docs.text: The place is a familiar part of daily life and a useful point of reference for visitors. Its value comes from the ordinary work, meetings, and routines that happen there rather than from a single famous event.

docs.title: The Fourty Knights
docs.text:
The Fourty Knights is the largest tavern and inn in Port Quartz, standing close enough to the docks that river crews can hear its busiest nights from the water.

Prance Mondrel owns the establishment.

docs.title: Character
docs.text:
The Fourty Knights is large, useful, noisy, and never quite as clean as Prance insists it is.

Merchants, ferrymen, guides, caravan guards, Legion soldiers, explorers, and dock workers all use the common room, which makes it one of the easiest places in town to hear news from several directions at once.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
The inn provides:

  • Rooms at several prices
  • Food and drink
  • Stable arrangements
  • Meeting rooms
  • Message delivery
  • Help finding laborers, guides, or escorts

Prance’s servants perform most of the actual work while he supervises from a chair whenever possible.

docs.title: The Quartz Cobra
docs.text:
The Quartz Cobra is Port Quartz’s sole Guild-chartered gambling hall and its Bank of Saros.

Pale stone scales curve around the doorway, while a long quartz cobra coils above the counting cage inside. Lind Bergy owns and operates the hall.

docs.title: Gambling
docs.text: The Cobra favors compact games suited to sailors, caravan crews, and merchants waiting on a ferry. Declared odds and stakes are written where all participants can see them. High-value private rooms overlook the river without providing a route to it.

docs.title: Banking
docs.text: The secured lower rooms accept deposits, store valuables, honor verified Guild drafts, exchange coin, and arrange withdrawals through other Guild halls. River schedules make the hall especially valuable to merchants who do not want their entire payroll sitting on a delayed wagon.

docs.title: Vane Archive
docs.text:
The Vane Archive is Port Quartz’s principal collection of expedition journals, route notes, ferry records, old surveys, and disputed maps.

It began as records preserved by the family of Edric Vane and gradually absorbed material from other explorers and civic offices.

Nelra Vossin is the current keeper.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
The archive includes:

  • Edric Vane’s surviving expedition journals
  • River-level records
  • Old crossing descriptions
  • Missing expedition lists
  • Copies of private maps
  • Merchant route notes
  • Travelers’ reports
  • Records of places that no longer exist

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
Nelra marks sources according to how directly they can be verified.

A drunken story may still be preserved, but it is not filed beside a measured survey without explanation.

The archive is especially useful because it separates centuries-old records from recent folklore concerning Rom and a supposed moving hill.

docs.title: Westwater Ferry
docs.text:
Westwater Ferry is the principal western river crossing at Port Quartz.

Heavy wagon ferries, smaller passenger boats, a fortified watch post, stables, equipment sellers, and a missing-person board surround the landing.

Oren Bale is the senior ferrymaster.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
Travelers arriving from Goslow or Kylor may use Westwater as part of ordinary regional travel.

People turning northwest toward The Masys Mountains also cross here, but the ferry should not be mistaken for the start of a safe road.

The last fragments of maintained path soon give way to the trails collectively known as Surveyors’ Step.

docs.title: The Vane Marker
docs.text:
A weathered marker commemorating Edric Vane points northwest.

The marker is older than the modern legends of Rom and a moving hill, and reflects Vane’s historical expedition route rather than either story.

docs.title: Practical Rule
docs.text:
Westwater can place a traveler on the correct bank.

What happens after that is no longer the ferrymaster’s promise.

docs.title: White Quays
docs.text:
The White Quays are the principal commercial waterfront of Port Quartz, carved into broad shelves of pale quartz.

Rain and river spray make the stone shine beneath lantern light, giving arriving travelers one of the town’s most distinctive views.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text:
The quays handle:

  • Passenger ferries
  • Cargo loading
  • Customs inspections
  • Rivercraft repair
  • Auctions
  • Animal transfers
  • Warehousing
  • Catch crews delivering recovered goods from Cataract Yard

Signal bells from Chainwatch coordinate ferry movements and warn crews about dangerous debris or sudden closures.

docs.title: Local Importance
docs.text: The White Quays are public ground and one of the few places where merchants, laborers, civic officials, Legion soldiers, river crews, and foreign travelers constantly mix.

docs.title: Caldus Renn
docs.text:
Caldus Renn is one of the few living guides known to have crossed the western rivers and returned from the foothills of The Masys Mountains.

He no longer accepts commissions.

Caldus walks with a stiff left leg and ties small river stones into his bootlaces. He claims they remind him which side of a crossing he entered from.

docs.title: His Final Expedition
docs.text:
Within the last few decades, Caldus found corrupted woodland, a circle of inexplicably healthy flowers, and a distant rounded shape that was gone the following morning.

Two companions vanished after following lights uphill.

Caldus does not claim to have met Rom, but his account is one of the stronger recent pieces of evidence that something strange moves through the Masys country.

docs.title: Captain Serin Holt
docs.text:
Captain Serin Holt commands the Aegis Legion garrison in Port Quartz.

He is controlled, observant, and more bureaucratic than Vostin The Mighty. Where Vostin tends to make a decision and accept responsibility for it, Holt prefers clear chains of command and written authority.

docs.title: Role
docs.text:
Holt is responsible for military security around one of northern Saros’s most important river crossings.

His garrison deals with:

  • Crown threats
  • Military cargo
  • Smuggling with strategic implications
  • Wanted fugitives
  • Road and ferry emergencies
  • Support for Legion patrols outside town

Ordinary civil policing remains the responsibility of Port Quartz rather than the garrison.

docs.title: Relationship with Hesta Vane
docs.text:
Hesta Vane and Holt agree that Port Quartz must remain secure. They frequently disagree about what security allows the Legion to do.

Holt thinks Hesta sometimes lets charter procedure interfere with urgent action. Hesta thinks Holt sometimes treats urgency as a substitute for lawful authority.

docs.title: Vostin
docs.text:
Holt has a poor professional relationship with Vostin The Mighty.

He considers Vostin too locally minded and too comfortable interpreting orders rather than simply transmitting them. A token or personal coin bearing Vostin’s mark may earn recognition and basic courtesy from Holt, but he does not treat it as a command, warrant, or special authority in Port Quartz.

docs.title: Hesta Vane
docs.text:
Hesta Vane is the First Mooring of Port Quartz and the presiding official of the Mooring Council.

A former ferry captain in her late fifties, Hesta is broad-shouldered, weathered, and missing two fingers from an old chain accident. She dresses plainly for ordinary work.

When ceremony demands formal office dress, she wears the purple cloak of office traditionally associated with Crown-recognized civic authority in Saros.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
Hesta is practical rather than charming. She has spent too many years around river accidents, cargo disputes, bad weather, and ambitious merchants to be impressed by titles alone.

She tends to reduce political arguments to material questions: who is being fed, who is doing the work, what is moving, what is blocked, and who will pay when something fails.

docs.title: Edric Vane
docs.text:
Hesta is a direct descendant of Edric Vane, whose expedition toward The Masys Mountains became one of Port Quartz’s great frontier stories.

She dislikes romantic retellings that erase the expedition’s cost.

“Edric Vane went west with sixty people. Seven returned. The statues always leave that part off.”

The Vane family helped preserve the material that eventually became the Vane Archive.

docs.title: Authority
docs.text:
As First Mooring, Hesta presides over matters involving:

  • Ferry and quay regulation
  • Salvage and fall-cask claims
  • Customs disputes
  • Emergency stores
  • Civic hearings
  • Town-charter conflicts with outside authorities

She recognizes the Crown but is fiercely protective of the legal rights granted to Port Quartz.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
Captain Serin Holt commands the local Legion garrison. The two cooperate when necessary and argue whenever military convenience threatens to become civic law.

Nelra Vossin manages the Vane Archive, while Oren Bale is one of the ferrymasters Hesta trusts most.

docs.title: Lind Bergy
docs.text:
Lind Bergy owns and operates The Quartz Cobra, the chartered gambling hall and Bank of Saros in Port Quartz.

Lind is quiet, immaculately organized, and gifted at remembering odds, faces, and unpaid promises. He dislikes theatrical threats because they slow the room down. A soft question from Lind usually means he already knows the answer and is measuring the lie.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
Lind treats gambling as entertainment, banking as trust, and cheating as vandalism against both. He will extend a modest courtesy to a traveler with a sound reputation and refuse a fortune to someone likely to endanger the hall.

He enjoys wagers that reveal judgment rather than wealth: weather, river timing, cargo weights, and whether a proud person can walk away.

docs.title: Nelra Vossin
docs.text:
Nelra Vossin is the keeper of the Vane Archive in Port Quartz.

She is soft-spoken, exacting, and far more interested in whether a story can be independently supported than whether it is exciting.

docs.title: Work
docs.text:
Nelra compares:

  • Expedition journals
  • Ferry declarations
  • Missing-person records
  • Cargo logs
  • Old maps
  • Merchant ledgers
  • Travelers’ accounts
  • Copies of documents whose originals have vanished

Her work makes the archive useful to explorers, merchants, historians, and officials who need to know whether a route or story has appeared before.

docs.title: Rom and the Moving Hill
docs.text:
Nelra is careful about chronology.

Edric Vane lived centuries before stories of Rom appeared in the Masys region, and his surviving records contain nothing about wandering homes or moving hills.

Accounts resembling the modern Rom legend appear only within roughly the last eighty years.

That distinction is important to Nelra because it separates old geography from newer folklore.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: She is patient with ignorance and impatient with carelessness. Wet fingers on an old page will offend her more reliably than an insult.

docs.title: Oren Bale
docs.text:
Oren Bale is the senior ferrymaster at Westwater Ferry in Port Quartz.

He is responsible for deciding when wagons, animals, passengers, and expedition parties can safely cross the main river.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
Oren is patient with fear and impatient with bravado.

People who admit they do not know the river receive advice. People who insist the river cannot possibly be as dangerous as everyone says receive much shorter advice.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
Oren knows:

  • How rainfall changes the western landings
  • Which ferry crews can handle animals or heavily loaded wagons
  • Where the maintained western path ends
  • Which expedition parties returned by a different route than the one they declared
  • How to read debris, color, and speed in the water

He has not personally traveled deep into The Masys Mountains, and he does not pretend otherwise.

“Once the river is behind you, every trail is somebody’s guess.”

docs.title: Prance Mondrel
docs.text:
Prance Mondrel owns and operates The Fourty Knights, the largest tavern and inn on the docks of Port Quartz.

Prance is famously lazy. He spends a large portion of each day in an oversized chair directing servants, complaining about expenses, and explaining to customers why whatever insect they just saw is either harmless, temporary, or technically someone else’s responsibility.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
Prance is loud, shameless, and much more observant than his behavior suggests.

He dislikes physical work but has an excellent memory for faces, tabs, room numbers, arguments, and who arrived in town with whom.

docs.title: Business
docs.text:
The Fourty Knights succeeds because Prance understands travelers.

He keeps enough rooms, food, drink, stable arrangements, and hired help available that merchants and expedition parties tolerate the tavern’s rough edges.

Prance is a member of the Merchant’s Guild, though his idea of respectable commerce is broader than some guild members would prefer.

docs.title: Pyrris
docs.text:
Pyrris is the capital of Saros, but it is not a large conventional city. It is a fortified royal settlement built atop an immense sheer cliff overlooking Bishop’s Bay, centered almost entirely around The Radiant Citadel.

Only about eleven hundred people reside there permanently. Most are members of the royal household, Council staff, scribes, diplomats, priests, Legion officers, servants, craftspeople, and the families required to keep the capital operating.

Visitors can make the population swell dramatically during festivals, petitions, royal hearings, and times of crisis.

docs.title: Character
docs.text:
Pyrris is formal, vertical, windy, and inconvenient.

Space within the walls is precious. Food must be brought in, water carefully stored, and almost every permanent resident has some relationship to the Crown or the Citadel.

For ordinary Sarosians, visiting Pyrris is often a once-in-a-lifetime journey made to petition Queen Amara, seek judgment, attend ceremony, or witness The Spring Harvest Festival.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
The only normal public approach is The High Road, a massive switchback road climbing from the direction of Goslow. The ascent can consume most of a travel day even when the road is open and weather is favorable.

Pyrris is heavily dependent on Goslow for food, timber, manufactured goods, travelers, and access to the wider trade network.

The cliffs also descend directly into Bishop’s Bay. Crown and Legion patrols maintain restricted waters below the capital, and ordinary vessels are kept well away from protected royal infrastructure.

Queen’s Gate is the guarded waterline approach below the cliffs. It serves royal and military needs and is not a public harbor.

docs.title: Travel and Supply
docs.text:
The High Road route from Goslow is approximately 35-40 miles. It takes about 2 days on foot, 2-3 days by loaded wagon, or 1 very long day to 2 days mounted. A griffin can make the journey in roughly 2-3 hours.

Food arriving from Goslow includes grain, vegetables, livestock products, and preserved seafood from Bishop’s Bay. The cost and difficulty of moving every ordinary necessity up the cliff are major reasons Pyrris remains a small fortress-capital.

See Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population for the canonical route model.

docs.title: Government
docs.text:
Pyrris is the seat of Queen Amara and Council.

Since the Queen’s disappearance, the Council has continued issuing decrees in her name while General Ironclad and the Aegis Legion maintain order.

The city’s small permanent population means the capital functions more like an enormous royal fortress and administrative center than a self-sustaining urban economy.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• The Citadel walls and inner guards
  • Stonepeak, commanded by General Ironclad
  • Checkpoints controlling the High Road
  • Restricted air and water approaches
  • Legion patrols around the cliff and bay

docs.title: Places of Interest
docs.text:
• The Radiant Citadel — the great white tower and royal seat
  • Stonepeak — Legion garrison and primary public checkpoint
  • The High Road — the public road connecting Pyrris to the Goslow region

docs.title: Queen's Gate
docs.text:
Queen’s Gate is the guarded waterline approach beneath the cliffs of Pyrris. It is part landing, part lifting station, and part defensive checkpoint serving royal and military needs below The Radiant Citadel.

It is not a public harbor or a convenient shortcut into the capital. Ordinary commercial vessels passing through Bishop’s Bay keep clear of the restricted waters while Crown and Aegis Legion patrols watch the approach.

The principal public route into Pyrris remains The High Road.

docs.title: Stonepeak
docs.text:
Stonepeak is the principal Aegis Legion garrison in Pyrris and the command post of General Ironclad.

It stands below The Radiant Citadel at the point where visitors entering the royal district can be screened before reaching more sensitive areas.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Stonepeak contains:

  • Barracks
  • Offices
  • Armories
  • Holding rooms
  • Checkpoints
  • Command chambers
  • Guard quarters for the capital

docs.title: The Checkpoint
docs.text:
Travelers entering the Citadel precinct normally pass through Stonepeak-controlled security.

Weapons, declared business, letters of introduction, and unusual cargo may all receive scrutiny.

The garrison also supports security along The High Road.

docs.title: The Radiant Citadel
docs.text:
The Radiant Citadel is the royal seat of Saros and the dominant structure of Pyrris.

The enormous white tower rises from the cliffside high above Bishop’s Bay and can be seen from great distances in clear weather.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Citadel contains:

  • The royal household
  • Chambers of The Queen’s Council
  • Court offices
  • Records and archives
  • Guest quarters for dignitaries
  • Ceremonial halls
  • Protected magical and administrative spaces

Queen Amara traditionally resides here.

docs.title: Fortification
docs.text:
The Citadel stands within powerful walls and is guarded by the Crown and Aegis Legion.

Its height, cliff position, restricted approaches, and controlled access make it one of the most defensible inhabited places in Saros.

docs.title: Public Access
docs.text:
Most visitors to Pyrris never see the majority of the Citadel.

Petitioners, officials, messengers, and dignitaries are admitted only to the sections relevant to their business.

docs.title: Ambassador Skylark
docs.text:
Leonora Skylark is the diplomatic and public-facing member of The Queen’s Council.

Her traditional office is often called the Queen’s Hand, reflecting her role as the Crown’s most visible representative in matters that require charm rather than force.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Leonora has golden hair, a bright smile, and the carefully welcoming appearance of a person who understands that every public gesture may be remembered.

Her formal clothing favors diplomatic symbols and rich but restrained fabrics.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text:
Skylark is warm, articulate, and extremely difficult to surprise in public.

She has a talent for making hostile conversations feel civilized without actually surrendering anything important.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
Her office handles:

  • Formal diplomacy
  • Relations with semi-independent settlements
  • Public statements
  • Ceremonial correspondence
  • Visiting dignitaries
  • Management of the Crown’s image

Since Queen Amara disappeared, Skylark has had the impossible task of reassuring the realm without being able to produce the Queen herself.

docs.title: Archmage Starweaver
docs.text: Nisel Starweaver is the Minister of Arcane Affairs on The Queen’s Council.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: Nisel is a serene elf with silver hair usually worn in intricate braids. Her formal robes carry subtle magical effects rather than obvious ornament.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text:
She speaks slowly and precisely, often allowing other people to fill silence rather than rushing to do so herself.

Her calm reputation has led many petitioners to underestimate how firmly she can refuse them.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
Starweaver oversees matters involving:

  • Crown-sanctioned magical institutions
  • Dangerous arcane discoveries
  • Magical defenses
  • Advisers and court magicians
  • Diplomatic incidents involving magic
  • Regulation of certain restricted magical practices

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Mages outside the Crown disagree sharply about her.

Some see a careful scholar protecting the realm from magical catastrophe. Others see the person most responsible for deciding which kinds of magic the government is permitted to fear.

docs.title: General Ironclad
docs.text:
General Roland Ironclad is the supreme military commander of The Aegis Legion and the military voice on The Queen’s Council.

He resides and commands from Stonepeak in Pyrris.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Roland is an imposing, weathered man with a close-cropped beard and the posture of someone who expects rooms to organize themselves when he enters.

His military dress is immaculate without being decorative.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text:
Ironclad is disciplined, strategic, and rarely hurried in public. He listens longer than many people expect and then gives instructions with very little wasted language.

He takes the Legion’s motto—Honor, Heart, Homeland—seriously.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
As supreme commander, Ironclad oversees:

  • Realm defense
  • Legion doctrine
  • Garrisons
  • Strategic patrols
  • Senior officer appointments
  • Responses to major military threats

Officers such as Vostin The Mighty, Admiral Thainan, and Captain Serin Holt ultimately serve within the institution he commands.

docs.title: Current Position
docs.text:
The disappearance of Queen Amara has made Ironclad one of the most consequential people in Saros.

He publicly supports continuity of government through the Council and has not declared the realm under military rule.

docs.title: Gormley
docs.text:
Gormley is the most famous bard in Saros.

The halfling performer is known for singing, dancing, juggling, stage magic, comic storytelling, and the ability to turn a room full of people who dislike one another into an audience for at least one song.

docs.title: Touring
docs.text:
Gormley spends much of the year traveling between major settlements, performing new songs and collecting stories for the next tour.

His appearances can draw visitors from surrounding villages and are especially profitable for local taverns.

docs.title: Pyrris Residency
docs.text:
During the spring, Gormley traditionally resides in Pyrris for The Spring Harvest Festival.

He performs public concerts and, when the royal household is functioning normally, entertains guests at private feasts in The Radiant Citadel.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Gormley is popular enough that political figures regularly attempt to persuade him to write songs favorable to their causes.

He prefers songs that people will still want to hear after the politician is dead.

docs.title: Lord Goldhaven
docs.text: Cedric Goldhaven is the Treasurer and Keeper of Wealth on The Queen’s Council.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: Cedric is an older human with salt-and-pepper hair, finely tailored clothing, and a habit of looking at expensive objects as though he can already see their entry in a ledger.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text:
Goldhaven is calm, reliable in presentation, and rarely emotional about money.

He treats finance as infrastructure: grain reserves, road contracts, garrison pay, debt, tariffs, and shipping all matter more to him than piles of coin in a vault.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
His office oversees:

  • The royal treasury
  • Major tax policy
  • Crown contracts
  • Garrison funding
  • Emergency reserves
  • Large infrastructure expenditures
  • Financial negotiations with guilds and towns

Since Queen Amara disappeared, Goldhaven has become increasingly important because political legitimacy is difficult to spend, while soldiers and grain merchants still expect payment.

docs.title: Queen Amara
docs.text:
Queen Amara Tatami is the elven Queen of Saros, widow of Caelum, and one of the longest-lived rulers known to the realm.

She has ruled for roughly eight hundred years.

docs.title: Appearance and Presence
docs.text: Amara is remembered as an ethereal and regal figure whose presence seems touched by residual magic. Her long life, elven heritage, and considerable arcane power have made her as much a living historical symbol as a monarch.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
For most of her reign, Amara was regarded as:

  • Benevolent
  • Patient
  • Forgiving
  • Personally kind
  • Difficult for ordinary people to reach
  • Strangely distant from smaller political disputes

People from across Saros have traditionally traveled to Pyrris hoping to bring petitions or serious grievances before the Queen.

Her willingness to forgive made her beloved by many and frustrating to officials who wanted harsher punishment.

docs.title: The Council
docs.text:
The Queen’s Council has handled much of the realm’s daily administration for centuries.

It has long been an open secret that the Council exercises more practical control over taxation, military policy, diplomacy, intelligence, finance, and magic than the Queen’s public image suggests.

Amara’s authority nevertheless gave the system legitimacy that the Council alone does not possess.

docs.title: Caelum’s End
docs.text:
Amara and Caelum made one final attempt to turn their former pupil Silas Voss away from evil at Caelum’s End.

No one else witnessed it. Caelum and Silas both went over the frozen edge into the northern sea.

Amara returned alone to Pyrris, where she assumed her husband’s throne. She has never provided a complete public account of the fall, and no accepted evidence proves that either Caelum or Silas survived it.

docs.title: Disappearance
docs.text:
Amara has now been missing for months.

No public explanation has satisfied the realm.

Common theories claim she has been:

  • Imprisoned within The Radiant Citadel
  • Kidnapped
  • Overthrown by the Council
  • Taken by The Prism
  • Killed
  • Forced into hiding by an unknown threat

The Council continues to govern in her name.

docs.title: Spymaster Shadowcloak
docs.text: Elias Shadowcloak is the Minister of Espionage and Intelligence on The Queen’s Council.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Elias is a drow who favors dark, practical clothing and very little visible decoration.

He has the unnerving habit of appearing in rooms without anyone being certain when he entered.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text:
Shadowcloak is quiet, observant, and more interested in what people omit than what they say.

He rarely threatens anyone directly.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
His office manages:

  • Intelligence gathering
  • Counter-espionage
  • Covert Crown operations
  • Informant networks
  • Threat assessment
  • Discreet investigation of politically sensitive problems

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Ordinary Sarosians know almost nothing verifiable about his work.

That lack of information has produced a thriving body of stories in which Elias is responsible for nearly every unexplained arrest, missing letter, exposed spy, or badly timed secret.

docs.title: Rore
docs.text:
Rore is the largest openly independent city in eastern Saros and a place where nearly anything can be wagered, financed, sold, hidden, or made respectable after enough paperwork and coin.

The Crown calls Rore unruly. Rore calls itself free.

docs.title: Character
docs.text:
The city is bright, noisy, cynical, and surprisingly organized. The Guild’s single chartered hall competes with unsanctioned house games and street games, lenders advertise beside taverns, private guards watch every profitable doorway, and a person can lose a year’s wages before breakfast if determined enough.

Rore’s independence attracts people who dislike Crown oversight as well as people who simply prefer looser rules.

docs.title: Government
docs.text:
The House Table governs the city. Great gaming houses, lenders, brokers, and ward representatives dominate the council.

Cassia Rook serves as First Dealer, the closest office Rore accepts to a mayor.

There is no permanent Aegis Legion garrison inside Rore. Crown officers may enter on official business, but the city does not recognize their authority over ordinary local civil law.

docs.title: Trade and Economy
docs.text:
Rore earns money through:

  • Gambling and gaming tourism
  • Lending and debt purchase
  • Coastal trade
  • Contraband brokerage
  • Entertainment
  • Private auctions
  • Money changing
  • Contract arbitration
  • Resale of cargo whose ownership has become inconvenient

The Gambler’s Guild is enormously influential but does not rule alone.

docs.title: Travel and Connections
docs.text:
The road to Trystn is a major long-distance corridor of roughly 150-170 miles: 8-9 travel days walking, 10-12 by heavy wagon, 5-6 days mounted, or 1.5-2 days by griffin.

Heavy trade with Ari usually prefers the coast. The journey takes about 1 day by coastal trader in favorable weather, compared with 4-5 days walking, 5-7 by heavy wagon, or about 3 days mounted.

See Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population for the canonical route model.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Rore is policed by ward guards funded by the major houses. Casinos, warehouses, lenders, and brokers also employ private guards.

Violence that interferes with business is punished quickly. Violence between people who knowingly entered dangerous arrangements receives much less sympathy.

docs.title: Places of Interest
docs.text:
• The Golden Goose — Saros’s largest gambling hall and Rore’s Bank of Saros
  • The Dealhouse — meeting hall of The House Table and seat of civic court
  • The Black Ledger — private brokerage house operated by Nessa Crowe
  • Salt Court — neutral arbitration hall for debts, contracts, and wagers

docs.title: Salt Court
docs.text:
Salt Court is Rore’s neutral arbitration hall.

Debts, wagers, shipping claims, private contracts, and disputes between people who do not trust Crown courts are settled here.

A ruling from Salt Court has no royal authority, but breaking one can make every major lender and gaming house in Rore refuse a person service.

docs.title: Local Importance
docs.text: The place is a familiar part of daily life and a useful point of reference for visitors. Its value comes from the ordinary work, meetings, and routines that happen there rather than from a single famous event.

docs.title: The Black Ledger
docs.text:
The Black Ledger is a private brokerage house in Rore operated by Nessa Crowe.

The public room looks respectable. The real business happens through coded ledgers, private appointments, bonded storerooms, and intermediaries.

Goods tied to pirates, forbidden magic, stolen noble property, or politically inconvenient owners can all find buyers here.

docs.title: Local Importance
docs.text: The place is a familiar part of daily life and a useful point of reference for visitors. Its value comes from the ordinary work, meetings, and routines that happen there rather than from a single famous event.

docs.title: The Dealhouse
docs.text:
The Dealhouse is the civic seat of Rore, where The House Table meets and the city’s public court is held.

The ground floor contains petition desks, record rooms, public notices, and court chambers. The upper hall holds the long table at which ward representatives, lenders, brokers, and commercial houses negotiate city policy under the eye of Cassia Rook, the First Dealer.

The Dealhouse handles crimes, civic disputes, licenses, and public law. Salt Court remains separate: it is a private neutral venue for contracts, debts, wagers, and commercial arbitration.

No gaming tables are licensed inside the Dealhouse. Rore’s government prefers to keep its metaphors from becoming evidence.

docs.title: The Golden Goose
docs.text:
The Golden Goose is the largest and most famous gambling hall in Saros. It is Rore’s sole Guild-chartered hall and also operates as a Bank of Saros.

Varo Quill owns and operates the Goose. Its licensed tables, tournament floors, counting rooms, kitchens, guest suites, and secured vaults fill a gilt-fronted building that never completely closes.

docs.title: Gambling
docs.text: The hall hosts public tables, professional tournaments, and private games whose stakes can include ships, businesses, and contracts. Guild rules protect the integrity of a declared wager; they do not protect a gambler from a foolish one.

docs.title: Banking
docs.text:
Like every chartered Guild hall, the Golden Goose is a Bank of Saros. It accepts deposits, honors verified Guild drafts, changes currency, stores valuables, and arranges withdrawals through other Guild halls.

The golden goose above the main doors is intentionally gaudy. Varo says anyone embarrassed by obvious bait should reconsider entering a gambling hall.

docs.title: Cassia Rook
docs.text:
Cassia Rook is the current First Dealer of Rore, presiding over The House Table from The Dealhouse.

She is polished, patient, and almost impossible to embarrass in public.

Cassia insists that Rore is not lawless. It simply refuses to let the Crown decide which laws are worth having.

She treats the Aegis Legion as a foreign military institution whenever its officers enter the city.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text: Cassia is polished without being warm. She lets other people make threats, then asks what outcome they actually expect. In Rore, that ability to separate pride from business is one reason she remains First Dealer.

docs.title: Nessa Crowe
docs.text:
Nessa Crowe operates The Black Ledger, a brokerage house in Rore that specializes in goods respectable merchants would rather not handle publicly.

Nessa does not ask where an object came from unless knowing its origin would change the price.

Pirates, smugglers, nobles, thieves, merchants, and occasionally officials all use her intermediaries.

docs.title: Rules of Business
docs.text: Nessa protects her reputation by being discreet, not sentimental. She will refuse cargo that is too dangerous to store, too famous to move quietly, or likely to bring every major faction in Saros to her door at once.

docs.title: Varo Quill
docs.text:
Varo Quill owns and operates The Golden Goose, the largest and most famous gambling hall in Saros. He is one of the most visible representatives of the Gambler’s Guild in Rore.

He sponsors tournaments, arranges high-stakes private games, and knows which visitors are gambling for pleasure and which are gambling because they desperately need money.

Varo is friendly to anyone who can afford to lose.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text: Varo treats conversation like a table game. He enjoys risk, notices desperation quickly, and prefers people who understand exactly what they are wagering. He is rarely the loudest person in a room, but he often knows who is losing before they do.

docs.title: Skaggerty
docs.text:
Skaggerty is an agricultural market town of roughly twelve hundred residents near Hex 62.99, standing where routes toward Goslow, Kylor, and the northern road country separate.

Its importance comes from both position and the broad belt of fortified farms, villages, mills, and seasonal holdings that use its scales and storehouses.

docs.title: Character
docs.text:
Skaggerty is small enough that unfamiliar travelers are noticed. Grain carts, small herds, road dust, and the bells of Temple of Austerus are more common than luxury caravans or military columns.

The settlement is surrounded by fields worked close enough to town that farmers can return behind the palisade before dark.

docs.title: Trade and Economy
docs.text:
Skaggerty primarily gathers, mills, stores, weighs, and exports grain and basic agricultural goods produced across its wider farm belt. The town’s population does not represent every farmer whose crop is sold under the Skaggerty name.

Inns, mills, granaries, teamsters, wagon services, and feed merchants benefit from the crossroads, but the town remains far less specialized than Goslow or Port Quartz.

docs.title: Travel and Connections
docs.text:
Goslow lies roughly 40-55 road miles away: 2-3 days walking, 3-4 days by loaded grain wagon, about 2 days mounted, or roughly 1 day for a fast courier.

Cargo intended for Port Quartz normally travels first to Goslow and is transferred to a ship. There is no ordinary safe commercial land route across the great rivers.

The northern road continues toward Dun Karag and The Masys Mountains, while local western routes connect toward Kylor. Exact mileages for those legs remain unsettled.

See Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population for the canonical route and population model.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: A modest palisade, local militia, and the occasional Legion patrol provide ordinary protection. The real defense is that Skaggerty is compact and its people know the surrounding land intimately.

docs.title: Places of Interest
docs.text:
• The Crossroads Weighhouse — council chamber, public scales, and office of Mara Sedge
  • The Stout Fool — the settlement’s only true inn and tavern, run by Simoon
  • Temple of Austerus — local temple overseen by Heldoren The Wise

docs.title: Temple of Austerus
docs.text:
A Temple dedicated to Austerus “The Shining One” located in Skaggerty. Deity of redemption and holy light, formerly the fiendish deity of searing radiance, now turned to Order. Seeks to bring all of humanity under one rule.

Heldoren The Wise oversees the daily operations of the Temple.

docs.title: Local Importance
docs.text: The place is a familiar part of daily life and a useful point of reference for visitors. Its value comes from the ordinary work, meetings, and routines that happen there rather than from a single famous event.

docs.title: The Crossroads Weighhouse
docs.text:
The Crossroads Weighhouse is Skaggerty’s public scale house, records room, council chamber, and emergency granary office.

The front bay holds a wagon scale and inspection floor. A stone-walled rear room contains the village charter, road assessments, harvest tallies, and sealed keys to communal stores. The upper chamber is barely large enough for the council table and whatever residents insist on attending.

Mara Sedge works here as Council Speaker and grain assessor. Notices posted beneath the awning cover road damage, livestock claims, militia watches, prices, missing goods, and meetings.

docs.title: The Stout Fool
docs.text:
Ran by Simoon, a diminutive and unassuming human male with quite an intellect and a dark sense of humor. He lives above the Stout Fool in one of the only few available rooms.

Rooms: (per night) Modest (1 sp) = 3 Accommodating (5 sp) = 1

docs.title: Everyday Use
docs.text: The establishment serves as more than a place to drink or sleep. Travelers use it to hear road conditions, find temporary help, arrange meetings, and learn which local businesses are actually open to strangers.

docs.title: Heldoren The Wise
docs.text:
Heldoren The Wise is the high priest of Temple of Austerus in Skaggerty.

He is an elderly, withered human, short and bent so severely by age that his cane seems to carry almost as much of him as his legs do.

docs.title: Duties
docs.text:
Skaggerty is too small to support separate specialists for every civic need.

Heldoren therefore serves as both priest and local sage.

People come to him for:

  • Religious rites
  • Old stories
  • Burial customs
  • Advice on unusual objects
  • Help reading older texts
  • Mediation when a problem is too personal for the village council

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
Heldoren moves slowly and speaks carefully.

He dislikes being hurried by travelers who have already spent several days creating a problem and suddenly require an answer before sunset.

His title “The Wise” began half as affection and half as a joke.

He has lived long enough that the distinction no longer matters.

docs.title: Mara Sedge
docs.text: Mara Sedge is the Council Speaker and official grain assessor of Skaggerty. She chairs the village council from The Crossroads Weighhouse, settles routine disputes, certifies wagon weights, and keeps the stores that matter when a harvest fails.

docs.title: Work
docs.text:
Mara’s ordinary responsibilities include:

  • Calling and moderating council meetings
  • Maintaining charter, tax, and road records
  • Certifying grain weights and resolving market disputes
  • Coordinating palisade repairs and militia watches
  • Releasing emergency grain by council vote
  • Speaking for Skaggerty to merchants, Crown officers, and nearby settlements

Her title carries more duty than grandeur. She still inspects scales herself and is often found with flour on one sleeve.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text:
Mara is practical, attentive, and slow to accept a comforting answer merely because everyone wants it to be true. She asks visitors what they know, what they inferred, and what they intend to do next.

She protects Skaggerty’s independence without pretending the village can solve every danger alone. A person who brings evidence and a workable plan earns her support quickly; a person who brings panic gets a chair, water, and several exact questions.

docs.title: Simoon
docs.text:
Simoon owns The Stout Fool, the only true tavern and inn in Skaggerty.

He is a diminutive human with a brash voice, sharp intelligence, and a dark sense of humor that works better on travelers than it does on everyone who has heard the same jokes for twenty years.

docs.title: The Stout Fool
docs.text:
Simoon lives above the inn in one of its few small rooms and is rarely far from the common room.

Because nearly every outsider in Skaggerty eventually passes through his door, he knows:

  • Which caravans arrived
  • Which road people used
  • Who is hiring labor
  • Who left town in a hurry
  • Which local dispute is about to become public

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
Simoon enjoys intelligent company and will happily argue with someone for an hour if business is slow.

He has little patience for customers who mistake a small town for an easy place to cheat people.

docs.title: Soryn's Crossing
docs.text:
Soryn’s Crossing is the principal trade junction of southern Saros, positioned where roads and waterways allow goods to move in several directions without first hugging the outer coast.

It is a commercial town before it is anything else.

docs.title: Character
docs.text: The Crossing is full of warehouses, ferry slips, stables, brokers, caravan yards, and temporary residents. The town’s population changes noticeably with the trading season.

docs.title: Government
docs.text: A charter council regulates tolls, quays, road maintenance, and market law. Dalen Soryn, a distant descendant of the family associated with the crossing’s modern name, currently serves as First Warden.

docs.title: Trade and Economy
docs.text:
Soryn’s Crossing makes money from:

  • Warehousing
  • Ferry and river traffic
  • Caravan services
  • Grain and livestock exchange
  • Money changing
  • Bulk resale
  • Repair and resupply

Goods from Mysha, the lake cities, the southern coast, and routes toward Ari frequently pass through the town.

docs.title: Travel and Connections
docs.text:
Mysha lies roughly 45-55 miles away: 2-3 days walking, 3-4 by wagon, about 2 days mounted, or 1-2 days for river freight when conditions cooperate.

Brynk lies roughly 40-50 road miles away: 2-3 days walking, 3-4 by wagon, about 2 days mounted, or less than a day by griffin. The climb makes bulky low-value freight expensive.

See Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population for the canonical route model.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The town maintains a professional watch and hires additional guards during major trade periods. Its strategic position also attracts frequent Legion patrols.

docs.title: Places of Interest
docs.text:
• The Great Crossmarket — central wholesale market
  • Soryn Hall — civic hall and toll office
  • Three Rivers Yard — secure caravan and freight compound

docs.title: NPCs Found Here
docs.text: NPC Race Building Factions Dalen Soryn Human Soryn Hall Merchant’s Guild

docs.title: Soryn Hall
docs.text: Soryn Hall contains the toll offices and council rooms of Soryn’s Crossing. Dalen Soryn conducts most public business here.

docs.title: Public Use
docs.text: Most residents encounter the building through ordinary civic business rather than ceremony. Notices, disputes, permits, records, and requests for local officials all pass through it, making the place a useful measure of what the settlement currently considers important.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
The Hall maintains toll books, warehouse licenses, caravan declarations, and road-maintenance accounts.

Because so much freight passes through Soryn’s Crossing, old records can reveal when a merchant, wagon company, or cargo route first began appearing in the south.

docs.title: The Great Crossmarket
docs.text: The Great Crossmarket is the wholesale heart of Soryn’s Crossing, where bulk goods change wagons, owners, and destinations.

docs.title: Everyday Use
docs.text: Trade here follows the rhythms of arrivals and departures rather than a fixed modern schedule. Prices can change sharply when a caravan, fishing fleet, or shipment is late, and local information often moves between stalls faster than it reaches any official notice board.

docs.title: Market Rhythm
docs.text:
Different portions of the Crossmarket specialize by day and season: livestock, grain, timber, tools, imported luxuries, or wagon lots.

Merchants use painted poles and hanging signs so caravan crews can locate the correct section even when the square is packed.

docs.title: Three Rivers Yard
docs.text: Three Rivers Yard is a secured freight compound in Soryn’s Crossing with guarded storage, wagon repair, animal pens, and space for caravans waiting on road conditions.

docs.title: Workday
docs.text: The site is busiest when goods are arriving, being processed, or being prepared for transport. Laborers, haulers, inspectors, and specialist craftspeople all depend on the work staying organized, so strangers wandering through active areas are noticed quickly.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Loaded wagons are assigned numbered spaces and sealed storage can be rented by the night.

The yard’s guards care less about the moral character of cargo than whether fees are paid and the declared owner can prove a claim if another merchant challenges it.

docs.title: Dalen Soryn
docs.text:
Dalen Soryn is First Warden of Soryn’s Crossing and a distant descendant of the family associated with the settlement’s modern name.

Dalen is a merchant-administrator more than a noble. He understands toll schedules, warehouse capacity, and caravan contracts better than ceremony.

He is usually willing to make a deal if the result keeps traffic moving through the Crossing.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text: Dalen’s family name carries history, but he works hard to avoid governing as though ancestry were a qualification by itself. Merchants generally consider him predictable, which in a trade hub is almost a compliment.

docs.title: Trystn
docs.text:
Trystn exists because roads meet there.

Caravans from Port Quartz, Lilya, Rore, and the central country all pass through the same broad corridor, turning the settlement into a town of wagon yards, inns, livestock pens, warehouses, smiths, wheelwrights, and arguments over whose cargo moves first.

docs.title: Character
docs.text:
Trystn is transient without being rootless. Many residents make their living serving people who will be gone by morning.

A visitor can hear accents from across Saros in a single market circuit. Wagon bells and livestock are as much part of the town’s sound as conversation.

docs.title: Government
docs.text:
The Crossroads Council governs Trystn under Elian Thorne, the Roadwarden.

Its authority is intensely practical: road maintenance, tolls, caravan space, market order, bridge repair, escort contracts, and disputes between merchants who may not even live in town.

docs.title: Trade and Economy
docs.text:
Trystn thrives on:

  • Caravan lodging
  • Wagon and wheel repair
  • Horses and draft animals
  • Grain exchange
  • Livestock markets
  • Warehousing
  • Toll collection
  • Escort contracts
  • Food and drink for travelers

It is also the safest conventional route between Port Quartz and Lilya.

docs.title: Travel and Connections
docs.text:
Destination Working Distance and Time Port Quartz 45-50 miles; 2-3 days walking, 3-4 by heavy wagon, or about 2 days mounted Lilya 60-70 miles; 3-4 days walking, 4-5 by heavy wagon, or 2-3 days mounted Rore 150-170 miles; 8-9 walking days, 10-12 by heavy wagon, or 5-6 days mounted

The long Rore road supports feed sellers, overnight stops, repair yards, and caravan staging throughout the corridor. See Saros - Distances, Travel, Trade, and Population for the canonical route model.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Trystn relies on its town watch, roadwardens, contract guards, passing mercenaries, and a small Legion patrol office.

The walls are less imposing than Lilya’s, but the constant presence of armed travelers makes the town difficult to intimidate cheaply.

docs.title: Places of Interest
docs.text:
• Four Roads Market — the great central open market
  • The Axle and Bell — busy caravan inn run by Jessa Marr
  • Tollhouse Commons — road office, public notices, and civic hearings
  • East Gate Caravan Yard — the largest secure wagon yard in town

docs.title: East Gate Caravan Yard
docs.text:
East Gate Caravan Yard is the largest secure wagon yard in Trystn.

Torv Hallick bases many of his caravans here. Freight bound for Rore often waits beside northern cargo from Lilya, making the yard a useful place to observe how goods actually move through the region.

docs.title: Workday
docs.text: The site is busiest when goods are arriving, being processed, or being prepared for transport. Laborers, haulers, inspectors, and specialist craftspeople all depend on the work staying organized, so strangers wandering through active areas are noticed quickly.

docs.title: Four Roads Market
docs.text:
Four Roads Market fills the center of Trystn with wagons, livestock, tents, grain, tools, and travelers.

Merchants from Port Quartz, Lilya, and Rore all use the market, making it one of the best places in Saros to hear conflicting versions of the same news.

docs.title: Everyday Use
docs.text: Trade here follows the rhythms of arrivals and departures rather than a fixed modern schedule. Prices can change sharply when a caravan, fishing fleet, or shipment is late, and local information often moves between stalls faster than it reaches any official notice board.

docs.title: The Axle and Bell
docs.text:
The Axle and Bell is a famous caravan inn in Trystn operated by Jessa Marr.

Its courtyard is large enough to lock down several wagons overnight, and its common room is designed around people who expect to leave before sunrise.

The inn is a reliable place to hire guards, drovers, and guides for the road toward Lilya.

docs.title: Everyday Use
docs.text: The establishment serves as more than a place to drink or sleep. Travelers use it to hear road conditions, find temporary help, arrange meetings, and learn which local businesses are actually open to strangers.

docs.title: Tollhouse Commons
docs.text:
Tollhouse Commons houses road records, public notices, toll disputes, and the offices of Elian Thorne and the Crossroads Council.

Large route maps cover the walls. Colored pins mark closures, monster sightings, missing caravans, and damaged bridges.

docs.title: Local Importance
docs.text: The place is a familiar part of daily life and a useful point of reference for visitors. Its value comes from the ordinary work, meetings, and routines that happen there rather than from a single famous event.

docs.title: Elian Thorne
docs.text:
Elian Thorne is the Roadwarden of Trystn and chairs the Crossroads Council.

He is less interested in ceremony than road conditions, bridge timbers, grain prices, and whether the next caravan will arrive before the last one consumes the available stable space.

Elian maintains working relationships with merchants from Port Quartz, miners from Lilya, and gamblers from Rore without trusting any of them completely.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text: Elian has the habit of asking where a wagon is going before asking who owns it. His priorities are movement, safety, and keeping one merchant’s urgency from blocking an entire road.

docs.title: Jessa Marr
docs.text:
Jessa Marr owns The Axle and Bell, one of the busiest caravan inns in Trystn.

She keeps a slate of arrivals and departures near the bar and can often tell who entered town, who left, and who quietly changed wagons in between.

Jessa dislikes violence inside the inn because broken furniture slows business.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text: Jessa is cheerful while business is orderly and frighteningly efficient when it is not. She remembers caravan captains, unpaid tabs, broken gates, and the exact stable a traveler used months earlier.

docs.title: Torv Hallick
docs.text:
Torv Hallick is a caravan master based at East Gate Caravan Yard in Trystn.

He organizes freight east toward Rore, west toward Port Quartz, and north toward Lilya.

Torv has recently seen unusually heavy sealed cargo traveling under official protection with paperwork too vague for its weight.

docs.title: Manner
docs.text: Torv is calm around ordinary delays and immediately suspicious of paperwork that hides weight, destination, or ownership. He has spent too long paying for other people’s bad manifests to find vague freight amusing.

docs.title: Delves
docs.text:
During the Second Age, dwarven and elven understanding of the Fey-Lines changed how both peoples interacted with the land.

Elven traditions used concentrations of fey-line power to cultivate life, conceal domains, and protect forests.

The Dwarven Clans built vast underground complexes at or near powerful convergences. Modern Sarosians call these structures Delves.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A Delve could combine:

  • Mine
  • Fortress
  • Clan settlement
  • Workshop
  • Storehouse
  • Fey-line installation
  • Access to deeper underworld passages

The dwarves sought valuable stone, metal, and Fey-stone while also establishing defensible underground centers.

docs.title: The Danger of Depth
docs.text:
Many delves were eventually sealed.

Dwarven stories repeatedly warn that a delve can go too deep, reaching places or creatures that should not be disturbed.

A large number of known delves are now abandoned, ruined, occupied, or lost entirely.

docs.title: Light and Abandonment
docs.text:
Working delves once used lamps, forge light, reflected shafts, luminous materials, or magic suited to their inhabitants. When those systems fail, the deeper works become truly lightless.

Explorers should not expect a centuries-sealed gallery to reveal more than their torch, spell, shard, or ritual light can reach. Beyond that small island of illumination, architecture and danger may remain completely unseen.

docs.title: Modern Delving
docs.text:
When a delve is rediscovered, adventurers arrive quickly.

Merchants, guards, laborers, scholars, and opportunists usually follow.

Some towns have grown around profitable old workings.

docs.title: Goslow Delve
docs.text:
Recently re-discovered and unsealed by an unknown source, a dwarf at The Toad has been leading adventurers into the cave entrance to the Delve under the assumption that his original party is all but lost down there.

A party of adventurers thwarted The Prism’s attempt to open the 2nd level of the delve that was sealed by magic centuries ago.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
The known entrance lies close enough to Goslow that the site has been explored repeatedly, but only the upper portions can be called familiar.

Collapsed passages, later occupants, and older sealed sections make every map incomplete.

docs.title: Importance
docs.text:
The delve is one reason scholars and adventurers in Goslow take dwarven ruins seriously rather than treating them as distant mountain stories.

Objects recovered from the complex occasionally reach specialists such as Bedford or the library at Temple of Torm.

docs.title: Port Quartz Delve
docs.text:
Port Quartz Delve is a known dwarven delve beneath or immediately adjacent to Port Quartz.

Unlike many rediscovered delves, it is not open to casual adventuring.

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
The accessible entrance is heavily guarded.

The Aegis Legion provides much of the physical security, while the legal right to admit independent explorers remains a source of civic sensitivity in Port Quartz.

Visitors normally require recognized authorization before entering.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Very little reliable information about the deeper interior is available publicly.

That secrecy has produced predictable rumors of treasure, sealed dwarven machinery, dangerous lower passages, and discoveries the authorities do not want ordinary people to see.

docs.title: Dungeons
docs.text: The settled parts of Saros are surrounded by ruins, tombs, forts, caves, sealed complexes, and other dangerous places collectively useful to adventurers as dungeons.

docs.title: Light Below
docs.text:
Abandoned Sarosian dungeons can be genuinely lightless. A sealed interior that has not been occupied for centuries does not retain ambient illumination merely to reveal its architecture.

A dying torch, lantern, spell, personal shard, or ritual source may expose only a small portion of a chamber while the rest remains absolute black. Occupied sites still use whatever practical light their inhabitants require; true blackout is a property of abandonment, depth, and circumstance rather than a universal visual filter.

docs.title: Tomb of The Serpent King
docs.text:
Tomb of The Serpent King is the ruined underground city and burial complex of The Serpent King, located several miles south of Goslow.

The site once belonged to a prosperous snake-man realm.

Time, collapse, occupation, and failed magical work have turned it into a dangerous ruin.

docs.title: Known Dangers
docs.text:
Stories and returning adventurers have associated the complex with:

  • Goblins
  • Blue mushrooms
  • Unstable chambers
  • Old snake-man architecture
  • Traps
  • The lingering work of Xiximanter

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
The Tomb is close enough to Goslow that would-be adventurers can reach it without mounting a major expedition.

That accessibility has made it famous.

It has not made it safe.

docs.title: Blackwater Bog
docs.text: Blackwater Bog is an enormous southern wetland whose dark water, drowned trees, and unstable ground conceal one of the great mass graves of the Second Age.

docs.title: The Dead
docs.text:
Stories of the Great Tribulation describe armies dying here in numbers too large to bury properly.

Bodies were piled into low ground, thrown into water, covered by mud, or simply abandoned where they fell.

Centuries of peat and black water have hidden much of the battlefield without truly consuming it.

Bones, weapons, armor, and old banners still surface after floods.

docs.title: Travel
docs.text:
The Bog is dangerous even without ghosts.

Hazards include:

  • False ground
  • Deep mud
  • Sudden channels
  • Insects
  • Poisonous plants
  • Rotting trees
  • Poor visibility
  • Creatures adapted to the wetland

Old causeways appear on some maps and vanish on others.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
The water is often described as unnaturally black.

Locals disagree whether the color comes from peat, ancient blood, magic, or all three.

Travelers tell stories of drowned soldiers walking beneath the surface and of voices calling from places where no solid ground exists.

docs.title: Caelum's End
docs.text: Caelum’s End is the northernmost point of Saros that can be reached on foot. The frozen peak ends at a sheer drop into the northern sea.

docs.title: The Confrontation
docs.text:
Public histories agree on only a few facts.

Caelum, Queen Amara, and Silas Voss were present. No one but Amara witnessed what happened.

Caelum and Amara made a final attempt to bring their former pupil back from the brink of evil.

Caelum and Silas both went over the edge.

Amara returned alone to Pyrris, where she assumed her husband’s throne.

Neither Caelum nor Silas has been reliably seen since. Amara has never provided a complete public account, so whether either fall was accident, sacrifice, or attack—and whether either man survived—remains disputed.

docs.title: The Common Account
docs.text:
Most Sarosians tell a simpler and more violent story: Caelum pursued his fallen pupil across the north, master and student fought until they reached the end of the world, and both plunged from the cliffs during their final struggle.

Court histories insist that Amara was present and that the journey began as one last attempt to turn Silas away from evil. Because Amara is the only known witness and has never told the complete story, neither version can be proven.

docs.title: Modern Importance
docs.text:
The remote peak became a historical and almost religious landmark despite its isolation.

Travelers who reach it find a cold, exposed region far removed from the political centers that still argue about what happened there.

The uncertainty surrounding Caelum’s final confrontation has only made the place more significant.
