docs.title: The Glimmering Expanse
docs.text:
The Glimmering Expanse is the vast central desert separating much of northern and southern Saros.

The region is not an ordinary sand desert.

Its dunes and flats are littered with razor-edged glass, fused sheets, crystalline ridges, and enormous formations that rise from the ground like broken transparent stone.

docs.title: First Age Scar
docs.text:
Sarosian tradition holds that the Expanse was created during the dragon wars of the First Age.

The nearby Wyrm Scar is considered the clearest physical evidence that those stories may describe a real catastrophe.

Whatever happened transformed an enormous region into a place where heat, wind, sand, and glass can destroy an unprepared expedition.

docs.title: Travel
docs.text:
Crossing the Expanse is considered one of the most dangerous overland journeys in Saros.

Hazards include:

  • Extreme heat
  • Lack of dependable water
  • Glass storms driven by high winds
  • Shifting dunes
  • Jagged fields that injure animals
  • Poor landmarks
  • Magical distortions
  • Long stretches without shelter

Few living guides will publicly claim they can cross the region and return.

docs.title: The Land Bridge
docs.text:
A narrow region of traversable land connects the northern and southern halves of the continent across the larger wound of Wyrm Scar.

On a map this can look like an obvious route.

In practice, reaching and crossing it requires surviving the Expanse itself, and the route is considered nearly unusable.

docs.title: Khaz’armok
docs.text:
Old stories claim the dwarven Khaz’armok once knew safe routes through the Expanse and may even have lived within it.

Modern Sarosians generally treat claims that Khaz’armok communities still survive there as tall tales.

docs.title: The Great Sphinx
docs.text:
Another persistent legend places The Great Sphinx somewhere within the Expanse.

No dependable map agrees on where.

docs.title: The Greyweald
docs.text: The Greyweald is the broad, ashen forest east of The Masys Mountains, north of Lake of Lament, and west of The Silvervein Summits. It is both haunted and deeply altered by fey magic.

docs.title: The Bent Wood
docs.text:
Grey bark, silver moss, and leaves that show the wrong season give the forest its distant color. Within the trees, paths loop without crossing themselves, dawn can arrive twice, and a traveler’s echo may answer before the traveler speaks.

The corruption is uneven. A glade may be harmless for decades and become dangerous in a single night. Elsewhere, a poisoned-looking grove shelters clean water while green and welcoming ground quietly leads people astray.

docs.title: Hauntings
docs.text:
Travelers report:

  • Lanterns carried by people who cast no shadow
  • Campsites found warm and empty, then found again miles away
  • Lost companions speaking from behind trees they could not have reached
  • Processions of old dead who ignore the living unless addressed
  • Fey revels that leave guests days or years from where they entered

Some spirits appear to be human dead. Others imitate human memory without understanding it.

docs.title: Travel Customs
docs.text:
Experienced travelers mark both sides of a tree, distrust straight trails, and never follow a familiar voice they cannot see. Iron bells, bread left at a fork, and sleeping with boots pointed outward are common precautions, though no custom works everywhere.

The Greyweald is not a single curse with a known center. Scholars suspect overlapping Fey-Lines, old violence, and centuries of isolation have created many smaller hauntings that now behave like one wilderness.

docs.title: The Urmong Barrows
docs.text:
The Urmong Barrows are a vast field of ancient burial mounds in southern Saros, raised during the wars of the Second Age.

Some are ordinary earthen tombs.

Others are so large that travelers mistake them for natural hills.

The greatest rise like small mountains.

docs.title: Origin
docs.text:
Tradition connects the Barrows to the worst human conflicts of the Great Tribulation.

Entire armies were buried rather than returned home, and later generations continued piling earth, stone, weapons, and dead atop older graves.

No surviving record agrees on how many bodies lie beneath the region.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
The Barrows are widely considered haunted.

Travelers report:

  • Lights moving between mounds
  • Voices beneath sealed stone
  • Empty armor standing upright at dawn
  • Animals refusing certain valleys
  • Old weapons appearing on the surface after storms
  • Paths returning travelers to places they already passed

Many stories are probably exaggerations.

Enough are not.

docs.title: Ani
docs.text:
The fortified coastal town of Ani exists partly because settled southern communities do not trust the Barrows to remain quiet.

Expeditions enter the region from Ani regularly.

Some return with old treasure.

Some return with fewer people.

Some do not return.

docs.title: The Wyrm Scar
docs.text:
The Wyrm Scar is the greatest visible wound in the geography of Saros.

The enormous canyon and watercourse nearly divide the continent into northern and southern halves, connecting the waters of The Sea of Myth and The Sparkling Sea through a broken central region.

docs.title: First Age Tradition
docs.text:
The Scar and The Glimmering Expanse are traditionally attributed to the dragon wars of the First Age.

The scale of the canyon is one reason even skeptical historians hesitate to dismiss the stories entirely.

docs.title: Passage
docs.text:
Travel through or around the Scar is extremely difficult.

Glass, broken rock, violent water, sheer walls, and unstable routes make ordinary navigation dangerous.

A land bridge exists across the greater divide, but it is surrounded by the Glimmering Expanse. Reaching it is usually more dangerous than the crossing itself.

For practical purposes, Saros’s northern and southern civilizations are connected by long routes around the central danger rather than a dependable road across it.

docs.title: Mountains
docs.text:
The mountain ranges of Saros contain mines, isolated settlements, old ruins, and entrances to forgotten Delves.

Mountain Region Region The Masys Mountains Saros The Silvervein Summits Saros Vy’Tungavor Saros

docs.title: The Masys Mountains
docs.text:
The Masys Mountains form the remote northern range beyond the settled roads west and northwest of Port Quartz. At Hex 53.85, Dun Karag guards the maintained passage through the range toward Caelum’s End.

Wide rivers, hills, broken forest, and difficult crossings isolate much of the region from the rest of northern Saros.

docs.title: Travel
docs.text:
There is no dependable road from Port Quartz into the western Masys country.

Explorers normally begin by crossing at Westwater Ferry and following portions of Surveyors’ Step before the trails disappear.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
The region is associated with:

  • Lost expeditions
  • Old ruins
  • Strange magical weather
  • Hidden valleys
  • Recent reports of sick or altered forest
  • The modern legend of Rom and a moving hill
  • The Greyweald, the haunted and fey-corrupted forest along the range’s eastern side

The Rom stories are comparatively new—roughly the last eighty years—and do not appear in centuries-old expedition records such as those of Edric Vane.

docs.title: The Silvervein Summits
docs.text:
The Silvervein Summits rise above Lilya and the high basin of Lake of Lament.

The Greyweald spreads west of the range, filling the haunted country between the Summits and The Masys Mountains.

The range is rich in mineral deposits and riddled with natural caves, worked mines, and older passages whose builders are not always known.

docs.title: Lilya
docs.text:
The mining town of Lilya exists because of the Summits.

Its economy depends on ore, stone, and materials pulled from the mountain, while its roads carry most normal freight south through Trystn.

docs.title: Old Workings
docs.text:
Dwarven construction has been found beneath and around active mines.

Some passages appear to belong to systems far older and deeper than current Sarosian mining.

How much of the range has truly been explored is impossible to say.

docs.title: Vy'Tungavor
docs.text:
Vy’Tungavor is a rugged eastern mountain region feeding rivers toward the southern interior.

The lower slopes contain scattered mineral claims supplied in part through Ari.

docs.title: Mining
docs.text:
Most operations near Vy’Tungavor are small compared with Lilya.

Prospectors establish temporary camps, work promising veins, and abandon them quickly when the cost of guards, food, or transport exceeds the value of the ore.

docs.title: Travel
docs.text:
The region is broken, steep, and poorly patrolled beyond the main approaches.

Old caves and ruined workings make it attractive to adventurers as well as miners.

docs.title: Griffins
docs.text:
The high peaks are the traditional origin of Sarosian Griffin Riders. A prospective rider normally enters the mountains to claim a fresh hatchling and begin the lifelong pair-bond there.

Unhatched eggs are exceptionally rare. The mountains’ scale, weather, predators, and inaccessible nesting country make every successful claiming dangerous, and many candidates return without a companion.

The tradition is not exclusive to any faction, although the Aegis Legion fields the most publicly visible riders.

docs.title: Surveyors' Step
docs.text:
The Surveyors’ Step is the collective name used in Port Quartz for the fading trails, cairns, hunter paths, and old expedition cuts beyond Westwater Ferry.

It is not a true road.

The Step only describes the first portion of the northwest route where generations of travelers have left enough signs that one can pretend a path exists.

A cracked expedition marker connected to Edric Vane stands near the last dependable portion.

Beyond that point, travelers heading toward The Masys Mountains are navigating wilderness rather than following a road.

docs.title: The High Road
docs.text:
The High Road is the enormous switchback road climbing from the Goslow region to Pyrris atop the cliffs above Bishop’s Bay.

It is the only normal public route into the capital.

docs.title: Travel
docs.text:
The climb is long enough that a journey between Goslow and Pyrris can consume most of a day even under good conditions.

Loaded wagons move more slowly.

Bad weather, inspections, damaged road sections, or heavy traffic can extend the trip considerably.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The road is strategically vital and closely watched.

Travelers pass Legion checkpoints associated with Stonepeak, and dangerous sections are protected by walls, gates, and reinforced turns.

Closing the High Road would isolate Pyrris from the supply network it depends upon.

docs.title: Bishop's Bay
docs.text:
Bishop’s Bay is the broad sheltered water shared by Goslow and the towering cliffs beneath Pyrris.

Its geography is one of the main reasons Goslow became the largest commercial city in Saros.

docs.title: Goslow
docs.text:
Ships entering the bay approach Goslow through waters complicated by local rocks and shallows.

Large vessels may anchor farther out while smaller craft finish cargo and passenger runs toward the city.

docs.title: Pyrris
docs.text:
The cliffs beneath Pyrris rise almost sheer from the bay.

The waters nearest the capital are heavily watched by the Crown and Aegis Legion, and ordinary vessels are discouraged from approaching the protected cliffside.

docs.title: Importance
docs.text:
Bishop’s Bay links royal power and commercial power more directly than almost any other body of water in Saros:

  • Goslow supplies trade and daily necessities
  • Pyrris supplies law, ceremony, and administration
  • The High Road connects them over land

docs.title: Lake Runa
docs.text:
Lake Runa is a southern inland lake surrounded by dense forest and old halfling traditions.

Families in Mysha preserve stories connecting their ancestors to the lake and treat it as more than a simple source of water.

docs.title: Character
docs.text:
Runa’s shoreline is heavily wooded, with stretches difficult to reach by road.

Fishing, herbs, small boats, and forest travel are more important here than large-scale commerce.

docs.title: Tradition
docs.text:
Halfling stories disagree on whether the lake was a refuge, birthplace, gathering place, or all three.

Many households in Mysha still preserve small customs associated with journeys to Runa.

docs.title: Lake of Lament
docs.text:
Lake of Lament occupies the high basin around The Silvervein Summits.

Beyond its northern shore lies The Greyweald, whose grey treeline fills the country between the Silvervein Summits and The Masys Mountains.

It sits far above the elevation of Port Quartz, fed by mountain water and drained through several channels.

docs.title: The Great Fall
docs.text:
At the lake’s southwestern edge, the water plunges over an enormous waterfall before becoming part of the river system flowing south toward Port Quartz.

The fall makes ship travel between Port Quartz and the lake impossible.

No vessel can climb it.

The violent downstream route is nevertheless used for one unusual kind of cargo: reinforced Fall Casks.

docs.title: Trade
docs.text:
Communities around Lilya can send small amounts of durable goods down the cataract in specially built casks.

Most normal freight still travels by road through Trystn.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
The lake is beautiful from a distance and dangerous at its edges.

Mountain weather can change water conditions quickly, and the outlet currents become increasingly violent toward the waterfall.

docs.title: The Sea of Myth
docs.text:
The Sea of Myth lies along the western side of Saros.

Its name reflects how little certainty Sarosians possess about what lies far beyond familiar coastal routes.

Kylor, Goslow, and other western settlements depend on coastal waters connected to the Sea for fishing and trade.

Sailors tell stories of distant islands, enormous creatures, strange weather, and lights beyond known charts.

Few captains are wealthy or reckless enough to test every story.

docs.title: The Sparkling Sea
docs.text:
The Sparkling Sea borders the eastern side of Saros.

In clear weather, mineral-rich shallows and bright sunlight give portions of the water a glittering appearance that inspired the name.

Eastern settlements such as Rore and Ari rely on the sea for fishing, coastal trade, and travel.

The same routes also attract smugglers and pirates, especially farther south toward Karastos.

docs.title: Sailing
docs.text:
The sea’s pleasant name does not mean harmless water.

Seasonal storms, reefs, piracy, and long stretches without a protected harbor make coastal knowledge valuable.

Captains traveling toward Rore, Ari, or the southern waters near Karastos pay close attention to local pilots and weather signs.

docs.text:
The seas, bays, lakes, and other named waters of Saros shape nearly every major trade route.

docs.title: R1. House Rules
docs.text:
1. No class/race restrictions & No bonus XP a. As long as the player can come up with a good reason for any strange combo… b. Bonus XP modifiers will not be used.

  2. Characters start with max HP a. Add CON +/- modifier. Players will still roll for HP at each level up.

  3. Slot-based inventory system a. Each character has an inventory of 10 slots +STR modifier bonus. b. Armor worn and weapons carried do not take up inventory slots. c. 100 coins = 1 slot / 1h items = 1 slot / 2h items = 2 slots / light armor = 1 slot / heavy armor = 2 slots / very small items = free carry / other items = referee’s discretion.

  4. Magic Users a. Start with: Read Magic, Light. b. Casting “Reversed: Darkness” still requires training in the Light spell. c. May use staffs regardless of class weapon restrictions.

  5. Fighters a. Cleave: Any time a fighter strikes a killing blow in melee they may immediately roll a free attack against another adjacent enemy within range. This can chain. b. May select a combat talent at 1st, 5th, and 10th level from the optional table (C.C. #1 page 28).

  6. Druids a. Start with: Speak With Animals

  7. Thief a. Optional rules from C.C. 1 page 29.

  8. Splintering Shields a. Characters can choose to destroy their shield rather than take the damage on a hit from a weapon or similar physical trap/spell/monster attack. b. If a shield is destroyed this way, the character incurs the “Fractured” de-buff. c. The “Fractured” de-buff causes characters to suffer a -2 AC and be unable to use their shield arm. d. The “Fractured” de-buff is removed when a character has fully rested and their HP returned to full.

  9. Downed, Recover, Wounded, and Character Death a. When reduced to 0HP characters enter a “Downed” state of 1. b. “Downed” characters can only perform a “Recover” roll (Save VS Death) on their turn. c. Recover Fail = Add 1 stack of “Downed”. Recover Success = Character moves to “Wounded” state. d. “Wounded” characters are returned to 1HP and are marked with the “Wounded” de-buff. This de-buff can stack. e. Healing a “Downed” character will return them to “Wounded” state. The heal restores HP as normal. f. The “Wounded” de-buff is removed when a character has fully rested and their HP returned to full. g. “Wounded” x3 / “Downed” x4 = instant death. ANY damage vs “Downed” = instant death. h. If at any time a character’s HP would be reduced by -10 + their character level they are instantly killed.

docs.text: Zero Tolerance (exception: Elves)

docs.title: 2. No Sexism
docs.text: Zero Tolerance

docs.title: 3. No Hate Speech
docs.text: Zero Tolerance (exception: Elves)

docs.title: 4. No Politics
docs.text: Unless it is about “The Council“…

docs.title: 5. No Sexual Themes
docs.text: No one wants to listen to your Spongebob fanfic…

docs.title: 7. No Bad Vibes
docs.text: If you aren’t feeling it, it’s okay to take a break or even sit out a session or two.

docs.title: 8. No Grandstanding / Session De-railing
docs.text:
Everyone will get their turn to be a hero. We are all here together so please try and focus on the game and honor the collective experience of others.

Everyone is welcome in Saros. If you can not agree to these rules this game/server is not for you.
